q: Fossil footprints, burrows and coprolites are collectively called:
why: Trace fossils (ichnofossils) record behaviour rather than body form. They can reveal gait, feeding and nesting even when no bones survive.
extra: The roughly 3.66-million-year-old Laetoli footprints show early upright walking hominins.

q: Denisovans were first identified from DNA in a finger bone from Denisova Cave in which mountains?
why: The 2010 genetic analysis revealed a previously unknown archaic human group. Their DNA is found in some modern populations, especially in Oceania and parts of Asia.
extra: A Denisovan jaw from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau shows they lived at high altitude.

q: Archaeopteryx fossils come from the Late Jurassic lithographic limestones of which region?
why: Fine-grained Solnhofen limestone preserved feather impressions in detail. The first skeleton was found in 1861, just two years after Darwin's Origin of Species.
extra: About twelve Archaeopteryx specimens are known.

q: Radiocarbon analysis of eye-lens proteins suggested Greenland sharks may live for roughly how long?
why: Eye-lens core proteins form before birth and are metabolically inert, so their carbon-14 content records the animal's birth period. A 2016 study estimated a minimum age of about 272 years for the oldest shark and a best estimate near 392 years.
extra: Greenland sharks reach sexual maturity only at around 150 years of age, according to that study.

q: The Sushruta Samhita is notable in the history of medicine for describing:
why: It describes surgical instruments and techniques including reconstruction of the nose using a skin flap. It forms a foundation of Ayurvedic surgery.
extra: The text was compiled over several centuries.

q: A 2010 genetic study of Tutankhamun's mummy found traces of which parasite?
why: The study suggested malaria and a bone disorder as contributors to his death. It also identified close family relationships among royal mummies.
extra: Howard Carter discovered his tomb in 1922.

q: The main eruptive phase of the Deccan Traps occurred about:
why: Deccan eruptions overlapped the end-Cretaceous extinction, and many scientists think volcanism added to environmental stress alongside the asteroid impact. The 252-million-year date belongs to the Siberian Traps.
extra: The Deccan lavas cover a large part of western and central India.

q: Near which English town did Mary Anning and her brother find the first correctly identified ichthyosaur skeleton in 1811-12?
why: Joseph Anning found the skull and Mary uncovered the rest of the skeleton in the Jurassic cliffs. Her later finds included a plesiosaur and a pterosaur.
extra: Her work on coprolites helped William Buckland recognise fossil faeces.

q: The Narmada skull cap found in 1982 at Hathnora, Madhya Pradesh, was recovered by:
opts: Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India
ans: Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India
why: The fossil is classified as archaic Homo, variously assigned to Homo erectus or Homo heidelbergensis. It remains the only well-known hominin fossil from the subcontinent of that age.
extra: It is dated to several hundred thousand years ago.

q: How does the platypus locate prey underwater, often with its eyes, ears and nostrils closed?
opts: Electroreceptors and mechanoreceptors in its bill
ans: Electroreceptors and mechanoreceptors in its bill
why: The platypus bill is packed with receptors that detect the weak electrical fields produced by muscle contractions of invertebrate prey. Together with touch sensors, they build a map of the surroundings.
extra: Platypuses are monotremes: egg-laying mammals found only in eastern Australia and Tasmania.

q: Which sun goddess is regarded as the divine ancestor of Japan's imperial house in the Kojiki?
why: The Kojiki (712 CE) records myths of creation by Izanagi and Izanami, and Amaterasu's grandson descending to rule. These stories legitimised the imperial line.
extra: Her main shrine is at Ise.

q: Which people carved the rose-red rock city of Petra?
why: The Nabataeans grew rich on caravan trade in incense and spices. They also developed sophisticated water-capture systems in a desert setting.
extra: Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE.

q: The tattooed mummies and felt textiles of Pazyryk in the Altai were preserved mainly because of:
why: Water seeped into the wooden burial chambers and froze, preserving skin, fabric and horse gear. The culture is linked to Iron Age nomads of the Scythian world.
extra: Tattoos include animal motifs, some stretching over entire limbs.

q: Su Song's astronomical clock tower of 11th-century China was notable for an early:
opts: Escapement mechanism in a water-driven clock
ans: Escapement mechanism in a water-driven clock
why: His tower at Kaifeng combined an armillary sphere, celestial globe and timekeeper powered by a water wheel. Its escapement regulated the movement.
extra: A model has been reconstructed in several museums.

q: Which Swahili city-state on an island off Tanzania built the Husuni Kubwa palace and minted its own coins?
why: Kilwa controlled the gold trade from Sofala in the medieval period. Chinese ceramics and coins have been found there.
extra: The Great Mosque of Kilwa is among the oldest on the coast.

q: The standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh was recovered mainly from the library of which king at Nineveh?
why: The Assyrian king assembled tens of thousands of tablets covering literature, omens and science. Excavators in the 1850s found them in the ruins.
extra: George Smith's 1872 announcement of the flood tablet caused a sensation.

q: Which region's art blended Hellenistic style with Buddhist subjects to produce some of the earliest Buddha images?
why: Gandharan sculptors depicted the Buddha with a Greek-inspired appearance. Mathura developed a parallel Indian tradition.
extra: Gandhara was in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan.

q: Why do some whales retain small pelvic bones?
opts: They are used for walking on land
They are vestigial remnants inherited from land-dwelling ancestors
They support the tail flukes directly
They are an artefact of fossilisation
ans: They are vestigial remnants inherited from land-dwelling ancestors
why: Vestigial structures reflect evolutionary history. Whale pelvic bones are not attached to the spine but anchor some reproductive muscles.
extra: Rare whales may even show tiny hind limb bones.

q: What is a qanat?
opts: A sloping underground channel tapping groundwater for irrigation
ans: A sloping underground channel tapping groundwater for irrigation
why: Qanats developed in ancient Persia and transport water by gravity over long distances with little evaporation. Maintenance shafts are spaced along the line.
extra: Related systems exist across Asia and North Africa.

q: Which early sauropod from India's Pranhita-Godavari valley is named after a famous poet?
why: Barapasaurus, from the Early Jurassic Kota Formation, was named in honour of Rabindranath Tagore. It is among the oldest known sauropods.
extra: It was described in 1975 by Jain and colleagues.

q: Epicurus taught that the highest good is:
opts: Ataraxia, or tranquillity, achieved through modest pleasures
ans: Ataraxia, or tranquillity, achieved through modest pleasures
why: Epicureans valued friendship and simple living and regarded fear of death as irrational. The school was based in a garden in Athens.
extra: Lucretius' poem 'De rerum natura' expounds Epicurean ideas.

q: Why do ichthyosaurs, sharks and dolphins have similar streamlined bodies?
opts: Common descent from a recent ancestor
why: Similar selective pressures for fast swimming led unrelated lineages to evolve similar shapes. Ichthyosaurs were reptiles, dolphins are mammals and sharks are cartilaginous fish.
extra: The shape is called fusiform.

q: Bronislaw Malinowski described the Kula exchange among which people?
why: Valuables such as armshells and necklaces circulate in opposite directions around islands. The exchange built alliances and prestige.
extra: Malinowski's fieldwork shaped participant observation in anthropology.

q: Lake Victoria's hundreds of haplochromine cichlid species are a classic example of:
why: A small ancestral stock diversified rapidly into many feeding and colour types. The lake itself is geologically young and dried out in the recent past.
extra: The introduced Nile perch drove many cichlid species to extinction in the 20th century.

q: Peter and Rosemary Grant's work on Daphne Major demonstrated what?
opts: Natural selection altering beak size in Darwin's finches during droughts
ans: Natural selection altering beak size in Darwin's finches during droughts
why: During drought years, finches with larger deeper beaks survived better because they could crack tough seeds. The changes were inherited by the next generation.
extra: Their study spanned several decades.

q: Why is the Indus script still undeciphered?
opts: There is no bilingual text, and inscriptions are very short
ans: There is no bilingual text, and inscriptions are very short
why: Around 400 signs appear on seals and pottery in short strings, so linguistic content is hard to establish. No long text or Rosetta-type inscription has surfaced.
extra: Indus seals have also been found in Mesopotamia.

q: Which technique uses tree-ring patterns to date wooden timbers?
why: Ring widths vary with climate, forming a sequence that can be matched across overlapping samples. A. E. Douglass developed it to date Pueblo ruins.
extra: Long ring sequences from bristlecone pines and oaks calibrate radiocarbon dates.

q: The 'island rule' predicts that large mammals isolated on islands tend to:
why: Limited resources and fewer predators favour smaller body size in large species. Dwarf elephants of Mediterranean islands and Stegodon on Flores are examples.
extra: Small mammals on islands often show the opposite trend, gigantism.

q: In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, which god slays Tiamat and forms the heavens and earth from her body?
why: Marduk's victory made him king of the gods and legitimised Babylon's supremacy. The epic was recited at the Akitu festival.
extra: The text takes its name from its opening words, meaning 'when on high'.

q: Homo floresiensis, found at Liang Bua cave in 2003, lived on which island?
why: The small-bodied hominin stood just over a metre tall and had a brain of roughly 400 cc. Its remains date to about 100,000 to 60,000 years ago.
extra: It was nicknamed the 'Hobbit' and may illustrate island dwarfism.

q: The Sutton Hoo ship burial, excavated in 1939, is generally linked to which Anglo-Saxon kingdom?
why: The burial's rich grave goods suggest a high-status ruler, possibly King Raedwald. The ship's wood had decayed, leaving an imprint in the sand.
extra: The finds include a famous helmet.

q: Caral-Supe, one of the oldest urban centres in the Americas (c. 3000 BCE), is in which country?
why: Caral is part of the Norte Chico civilisation, with monumental platform mounds and plazas. It lacks pottery, so it belongs to the preceramic period.
extra: Its economy was based on cotton, beans and fishing.

q: In Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, who survived the great flood and was granted immortality?
why: Utnapishtim built a boat on divine advice and saved his family and animals. He tells Gilgamesh the story and shows that immortality cannot be gained.
extra: The older Atrahasis epic contains a similar flood story with the hero named Atrahasis.

q: Which biologist championed serial endosymbiosis as the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts?
why: Margulis argued in 1967 that these organelles descended from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by host cells. Evidence includes their own circular DNA and bacterial-type ribosomes.
extra: Mitochondria are related to alphaproteobacteria and chloroplasts to cyanobacteria.

q: Titanoboa cerrejonensis, a giant Palaeocene snake, was found in which country?
why: Fossils came from the Cerrejon coal mine and date to about 60 million years ago. Estimates give it a length of around 13 metres.
extra: Its size has been used to infer high tropical temperatures of roughly 30 to 34 degrees Celsius.

q: Homo naledi, from the Rising Star cave system in South Africa, is notable for being:
opts: A small-brained hominin dated to around 300,000 years ago
A hybrid of Neanderthals and humans
ans: A small-brained hominin dated to around 300,000 years ago
why: Its mix of primitive and modern features, including a brain about a third the size of ours, surprised researchers. Fossils from the Dinaledi chamber were dated to roughly 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.
extra: Claims that it deliberately buried its dead are debated.

q: The Roman Lycurgus Cup appears green in reflected light and red in transmitted light because of:
opts: Gold and silver nanoparticles in the glass
ans: Gold and silver nanoparticles in the glass
why: The nanoparticles scatter and absorb light differently depending on viewing direction. This dichroic effect was achieved by Roman glassmakers around the 4th century CE.
extra: It is held in the British Museum.

q: Why has airborne LiDAR transformed archaeology in tropical forests?
opts: It penetrates vegetation to map the ground surface
ans: It penetrates vegetation to map the ground surface
why: Laser pulses reach the ground between leaves, creating detailed terrain models that show ancient structures. Surveys in Guatemala and Cambodia revealed tens of thousands of previously unknown features.
extra: A 2018 Maya survey identified over 60,000 structures.

q: Mosasaurs, the Late Cretaceous marine predators, are most closely related to:
opts: Squamates such as monitor lizards and snakes
ans: Squamates such as monitor lizards and snakes
why: Mosasaurs evolved from lizard-like ancestors and became top predators in the oceans. They are not dinosaurs.
extra: They died out at the K-Pg extinction about 66 million years ago.

q: Which Gujarat Harappan site is often cited as having evidence of a tidal dock or basin?
why: Lothal's brick basin is thought to have served maritime trade, though some scholars interpret it as an irrigation tank. The site also has bead-making workshops.
extra: The site is proposed for a national maritime heritage complex.

q: The Bhimbetka rock shelters, with paintings ranging from the Mesolithic to medieval times, are in which state?
why: V.S. Wakankar identified the site in 1957-58. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has hundreds of painted shelters.
extra: Some Acheulean tools there are far older than the paintings.

q: Which Egyptian goddess's cult spread widely across the Roman Empire, with temples reaching Britain?
why: Isis worship combined Egyptian and Greco-Roman elements and attracted a broad following. Evidence for a temple of Isis has been found in London.
extra: She was associated with magic and motherhood.

q: Why is the name of Basilosaurus ('king lizard') misleading?
opts: It is an early whale, not a reptile
It was a lizard but not a king
It is a type of dinosaur
ans: It is an early whale, not a reptile
why: This Eocene cetacean, about 34 to 40 million years ago, had a long snake-like body and tiny hind limbs. Early naturalists wrongly assumed it was a reptile.
extra: Its vestigial legs show whales evolved from land mammals.

q: Dunkleosteus, a giant Devonian predator, killed prey using:
opts: Self-sharpening bony blades instead of true teeth
ans: Self-sharpening bony blades instead of true teeth
why: This placoderm had bony plates in its jaws that wore into sharp edges. It could open its mouth extremely quickly to create suction.
extra: It reached lengths of several metres about 360 million years ago.

q: Which songbird complex around the Tibetan Plateau is a well-studied possible ring species?
why: Populations around the plateau interbreed with neighbours but the ends of the ring, overlapping in Siberia, do not. Irwin and colleagues studied song and genetic divergence.
extra: Ring species show how gradual divergence can result in reproductive isolation.

q: The Newgrange passage tomb in Ireland is aligned to which event?
why: A roof-box above the entrance lets the rising sun light the inner chamber for a few minutes around the solstice. It was built around 3200 BCE.
extra: Newgrange is older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid.

q: Quetzalcoatlus northropi, with a wingspan of about 10 to 11 metres, was a:
why: Azhdarchids were long-necked, toothless pterosaurs that likely foraged on the ground. Quetzalcoatlus was named after the Aztec feathered serpent god.
extra: Fossils were found in Texas and date to the Late Cretaceous.

q: The Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947, include the oldest known manuscripts of:
why: Scrolls from caves near Qumran include nearly every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. They are over a thousand years older than medieval copies.
extra: The first scrolls were found by Bedouin shepherds.

q: Which Chinese pilgrim studied at Nalanda in the 7th century?
why: Xuanzang spent years at Nalanda and returned to China with hundreds of Buddhist manuscripts. His travel account is a key source on early India.
extra: Yijing also studied there.

q: Around 110 BCE, the Greek ambassador Heliodorus erected a pillar at Besnagar in honour of:
why: The inscription on the Garuda pillar calls Heliodorus a devotee of Vasudeva and a Bhagavata. It shows Greek adoption of an Indian devotional tradition.
extra: The pillar is near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh.

q: Which shared feature with birds helped sauropods reduce skeletal weight while growing enormous?
why: Sauropod vertebrae contained cavities from air sacs connected to an efficient respiratory system. This lowered weight and supported long necks.
extra: Argentinosaurus is estimated at 70 tonnes or more.

q: Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, dated to about 9500 BCE, challenges the idea that:
opts: Monumental architecture appeared only after farming and settled life
ans: Monumental architecture appeared only after farming and settled life
why: Hunter-gatherers raised carved T-shaped limestone pillars before clear evidence of farming at the site. Klaus Schmidt led excavations from 1995.
extra: It is near Sanliurfa in southeastern Turkey.

q: Zhang Heng's invention of 132 CE in Han China was a:
why: His bronze vessel with dragon heads and toad mouths indicated the direction of distant earthquakes. The exact mechanism is debated.
extra: Zhang Heng was also an astronomer and mathematician.

q: Originally, the Terracotta Army warriors were:
why: Lacquer and mineral pigments coloured the figures, but the paint flaked off rapidly when exposed to air after excavation. Traces remain on some figures.
extra: Farmers digging a well found the army in 1974 near Xi'an; it guards the tomb of Qin Shi Huang.

q: Which lake, the world's deepest and oldest freshwater lake at roughly 25 million years, is home to the endemic Baikal seal?
why: Lake Baikal occupies a rift valley in Siberia, reaches over 1,600 m in depth and holds a large share of the planet's liquid surface freshwater. Its long isolation produced many endemic species.
extra: Baikal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: How did scientists date the Norse presence at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland precisely to 1021 CE?
opts: Tree rings combined with a cosmic-ray spike in 993 CE
ans: Tree rings combined with a cosmic-ray spike in 993 CE
why: Wood cut with metal tools showed a radiocarbon spike linked to a solar event in 993 CE. Counting rings from this marker gave a cutting year of 1021.
extra: This is the first precisely dated evidence of Europeans in the Americas.

q: Which Moroccan traveller served as a judge in Delhi under Muhammad bin Tughluq?
why: He spent several years in India in the 1330s and left detailed accounts of the court. His Rihla describes travels across Africa and Asia.
extra: He later travelled to the Maldives and China.

q: True or false: modern archaeologists generally accept that Mohenjo-daro was destroyed by a single massacre by Aryan invaders.
why: Mortimer Wheeler's 1940s idea was based on a few skeletal finds scattered at different levels. Later analysis showed that they did not represent a single massacre.
extra: Evidence points to a gradual decline of the Indus cities.

q: Early proto-cuneiform tablets at Uruk (c. 3400-3200 BCE) were mainly used for:
why: The earliest writing recorded quantities of grain, livestock and rations. Literary use developed later.
extra: Writing may have grown out of clay token systems.

q: True or false: pterosaurs such as Pteranodon are classified as dinosaurs.
why: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles that were close relatives of dinosaurs, both being ornithodirans. They are not dinosaurs, nor were they ancestors of birds.
extra: Marine reptiles such as ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are not dinosaurs either.

q: Which Gujarat area near Balasinor is known for one of the largest dinosaur nesting and egg-fossil sites in the world?
why: Thousands of fossil eggs and nests of titanosaur sauropods have been documented around Raiyoli. The site records colonial-style nesting in the Late Cretaceous.
extra: The Raiyoli site is promoted as a geopark and dinosaur fossil park.

q: Mungo Lady, from Lake Mungo in Australia, is notable as:
opts: One of the world's oldest known cremations
ans: One of the world's oldest known cremations
why: Her remains are about 40,000 years old and were burnt and crushed. Lake Mungo shows early human presence in Australia.
extra: Mungo Man was buried with ochre.

q: Jericho's early Neolithic settlement is noted for a massive:
why: The tower, dated to roughly 8000 BCE, stands about 8 metres high with an internal stairway. Its purpose is debated.
extra: Jericho is among the oldest continuously inhabited places.

q: The Gathas, ascribed to Zarathustra, form part of which sacred text?
why: The Gathas are the oldest layer of the Avesta, composed in Old Avestan. They emphasise the choice between truth (asha) and falsehood (druj).
extra: The Bundahishn is a later Zoroastrian text.

q: In 2022, LiDAR revealed low-density urbanism of which Amazonian culture in Bolivia?
why: The Llanos de Mojos has platform mounds, causeways and reservoirs, dating to between about 500 and 1400 CE. It showed that complex societies existed in the Amazon.
extra: The study was published in Nature.

q: Chaco Canyon, with great houses like Pueblo Bonito, is located in which US state?
why: It was a hub of Ancestral Puebloan culture from about 850 to 1150 CE. Roads radiate out from the canyon.
extra: Residue analysis has shown that cacao was consumed there.

q: Angkor Wat was originally dedicated to which deity?
why: Suryavarman II built it in the 12th century as a Hindu temple. It was later converted to Buddhist use.
extra: It is considered the largest religious monument in the world.

q: Argentavis magnificens, a Miocene giant of Argentina, was a:
opts: Huge flying bird of the teratorn group
ans: Huge flying bird of the teratorn group
why: With a wingspan estimated at about 6 to 7 metres, it was one of the largest flying birds known. It probably relied on soaring over the grasslands.
extra: Teratorns were New World relatives of vultures and condors.

q: Who first recognised the unusual fish caught off East London, South Africa, in 1938 as something remarkable, leading to the identification of a living coelacanth?
why: Courtenay-Latimer, a museum curator, spotted the strange fish among a trawler catch and contacted ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith. He confirmed it as a coelacanth, a group thought extinct since the Cretaceous.
extra: The species was named Latimeria chalumnae in her honour.

q: Which Mesoamerican civilisation independently developed a positional number system with a symbol for zero?
why: The Maya used a base-20 system with a shell-shaped glyph as a placeholder. This was a separate invention from Indian and Babylonian zero.
extra: They also kept highly accurate calendars.

q: Mani, founder of Manichaeism, taught a dualism of:
why: The faith spread from Persia into the Roman Empire and as far as China. It held that matter is trapped in darkness and the soul must be freed.
extra: Augustine of Hippo was a Manichaean for about nine years.

q: Which cave in France, discovered in 1994, contains paintings about 36,000 years old?
why: Chauvet's paintings of lions, rhinos and bears are sophisticated, showing shading and perspective. The cave was sealed by a rockfall for thousands of years.
extra: Lascaux's paintings are about 17,000 years old.

q: Whose 1858 essay from Ternate prompted Darwin to publish on natural selection?
why: Wallace independently arrived at the idea of natural selection and sent a letter to Darwin. Their ideas were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in July 1858.
extra: Wallace also pioneered biogeography in the Malay Archipelago.

q: The Prose Edda, a key source for Norse mythology, was compiled around 1220 by:
why: Snorri, an Icelandic poet and politician, wrote it as a handbook for poets. It preserves many myths, including those about Odin, Thor and Ragnarok.
extra: The Poetic Edda is a separate collection of anonymous poems.

q: Wolbachia, a bacterium found in many insects, is notable because it can:
opts: Manipulate host reproduction, for example through cytoplasmic incompatibility
Fix atmospheric nitrogen for insect hosts
ans: Manipulate host reproduction, for example through cytoplasmic incompatibility
why: Wolbachia is passed through eggs and can bias reproduction in its favour by killing the offspring of uninfected females, feminising males or inducing parthenogenesis. This helps it spread rapidly through host populations.
extra: Releases of Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes are used to reduce dengue transmission.

q: Inca administrators kept records using:
why: Colours, knot types and positions recorded numbers and probably other information. Specialists called quipucamayocs managed them.
extra: Some scholars think certain quipus may encode narrative as well as numerical data.

q: The Kikkuli text, a Hittite-era document from about 1400 BCE, is the earliest known treatise on:
why: Kikkuli, a Mitanni horse trainer, set out a detailed training schedule for chariot horses. It contains Indo-Aryan-like technical terms.
extra: The Mitanni elite used some Indo-Aryan names and terms.

q: The Olmec colossal stone heads are generally interpreted as:
why: Individual features and headgear suggest distinct leaders. Heads were carved from basalt hauled long distances at sites like San Lorenzo.
extra: The Olmec are often called a 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica.

q: Which pre-Buddhist religious tradition of Tibet still survives and influenced Tibetan Buddhism?
why: Bon has its own rituals and monasteries. Tibetan Buddhism absorbed many of its deities.
extra: Mount Kailash is sacred in Bon.

q: Who deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's edicts in 1837?
why: Prinsep worked with inscriptions and coin legends to crack the script. The identification of 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' with Ashoka came later through Sri Lankan chronicles.
extra: A Maski edict of 1915 explicitly named Ashoka.

q: The Uluburun shipwreck off Turkey, dated about 1320 BCE, is notable for its cargo of:
opts: Copper and tin ingots, glass ingots and luxury goods
ans: Copper and tin ingots, glass ingots and luxury goods
why: The ship carried goods from many regions, illustrating Late Bronze Age long-distance trade. Raw copper ingots of ox-hide shape were common.
extra: It was excavated over a decade by underwater archaeologists.

q: In the Sumerian poem 'Descent of Inanna', what happens as she passes through the seven gates of the underworld?
opts: She is stripped of her garments and powers
ans: She is stripped of her garments and powers
why: At each gate she gives up an item of royal dress or power, arriving naked before Ereshkigal. She is then killed and later revived.
extra: Inanna is the Sumerian counterpart of Ishtar.

q: The Behistun Inscription helped decipher cuneiform. Which king ordered it?
why: It is written in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Henry Rawlinson copied it in the 1830s and 1840s.
extra: It stands on a cliff in western Iran.

q: Antarctic icefishes are unusual among vertebrates because they:
opts: Breathe atmospheric air at the surface
Lack haemoglobin and have clear, colourless blood
ans: Lack haemoglobin and have clear, colourless blood
why: Icefishes (family Channichthyidae) carry no haemoglobin; oxygen is simply dissolved in the plasma. This works in the cold, oxygen-rich Southern Ocean, helped by large hearts and wide blood vessels.
extra: They are the only known adult vertebrates without red blood cells carrying haemoglobin.

q: Which event cleared the way for dinosaurs to dominate Mesozoic ecosystems?
opts: The end-Triassic extinction around 201 million years ago
ans: The end-Triassic extinction around 201 million years ago
why: The Triassic-Jurassic extinction wiped out many large competitors among the archosaurs, such as other crurotarsans. Dinosaurs then diversified rapidly in the Jurassic.
extra: Eruptions of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province are linked to this event.

q: NAGPRA, enacted in the United States in 1990, concerns the:
opts: Repatriation of Native American human remains and sacred objects
ans: Repatriation of Native American human remains and sacred objects
why: The law requires federally funded institutions to consult with tribes and return certain remains and cultural items. It reshaped relations between museums and Indigenous peoples.
extra: Many other countries debate similar repatriation questions.

q: Egyptian inscriptions at Medinet Habu record invasions around 1177 BCE by whom?
why: Ramesses III described defeating coalitions of seaborne raiders. These events fall within the Late Bronze Age collapse, which saw the fall of Hittite power and many Aegean and Levantine centres.
extra: Their origins remain debated.

q: The English word 'algorithm' derives from the name of which scholar?
why: The Baghdad scholar of the 9th century wrote on Hindu-Arabic numerals and on algebra. The word 'algebra' comes from al-jabr, a term in his book title.
extra: He worked at the House of Wisdom under the Abbasids.

q: In Hesiod's Works and Days, Pandora's 'box' was originally a:
why: Erasmus's 16th-century Latin rendering as 'pyxis' led to the familiar 'box'. In the myth the jar released evils into the world, leaving hope inside.
extra: Pandora was fashioned by the gods on Zeus's orders.

q: Dholavira in Kutch, a UNESCO site since 2021, is noted for:
opts: Sophisticated water conservation and a large Indus-script signboard
ans: Sophisticated water conservation and a large Indus-script signboard
why: The Harappan city used reservoirs and channels to manage scarce water. A large inscription of Indus signs was found near a gate.
extra: It is among the largest Harappan sites in India.

q: According to Parsi tradition, Zoroastrian refugees first landed in Gujarat at:
why: The Qissa-i Sanjan, a 16th-century account, recounts their arrival and negotiation with the local ruler. They became known as Parsis.
extra: Their descendants include many of India's prominent business families.

q: Critics of the 'ecocide' account of Rapa Nui's deforestation point to the role of:
opts: Introduced Polynesian rats that ate palm seeds
ans: Introduced Polynesian rats that ate palm seeds
why: Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo argued that rats prevented forest regeneration and that the population did not collapse until European contact. Their view is debated.
extra: Diseases and slave raids in the 19th century devastated the population.

q: Some of the oldest widely cited stromatolites, about 3.48 billion years old, occur in which Australian region?
why: These layered structures formed by microbial mats are found in the Dresser Formation of the Pilbara. Their biological origin is accepted by many but is still debated for the very oldest examples.
extra: Living stromatolites occur at Shark Bay in Western Australia.

q: The Delhi Iron Pillar resists rust largely because of:
opts: A protective passive film enriched by phosphorus in the iron
ans: A protective passive film enriched by phosphorus in the iron
why: The pillar, dated to the Gupta period, developed a thin film of iron hydrogen phosphate (misawite). The high phosphorus content and local climate helped the layer form.
extra: It stands in the Qutb complex, Delhi.

q: Mary Schweitzer's 2005 report of flexible, vessel-like structures in a Hell Creek fossil involved which animal?
why: After demineralising the femur of specimen MOR 1125, her team found soft-tissue-like structures that sparked debate over fossil preservation. Later work examined preservation of proteins and the role of iron.
extra: Initial claims of ancient proteins were contested and tested by other labs.

q: Hero of Alexandria's aeolipile is an early example of:
why: Steam escaping from bent nozzles on a sphere made it spin. It was a curiosity and not used for work.
extra: Hero also described automata and a vending device.

q: Where were Gnostic texts such as the Gospel of Thomas found in 1945?
why: A sealed jar of papyrus codices was found near Nag Hammadi. Their texts show diverse early Christian and Gnostic ideas.
extra: The discovery was made by a farmer.

q: Which anthropologist is often called the father of American anthropology and championed cultural relativism?
why: Boas argued that cultures should be understood in their own terms and challenged racial hierarchies. He trained many prominent anthropologists.
extra: He emphasised fieldwork and linguistics as well as culture.

q: Chemical analysis of fatty residues in Neolithic pottery has been used mainly to detect:
opts: Processed animal products such as milk
ans: Processed animal products such as milk
why: Lipids absorb into unglazed pottery and can be identified by isotopic signatures. This showed dairying in Europe by about 7,000 years ago.
extra: Residue analysis also reveals cooking of fish, meat and plants.

q: The Jiahu site in Henan, China (c. 7000-5700 BCE), yielded some of the oldest playable:
why: The flutes were made from the wing bones of red-crowned cranes and have multiple holes. Some can still be played.
extra: Jiahu also shows early rice cultivation and possible proto-writing symbols.

q: The Cyrus Cylinder was issued after Cyrus the Great captured which city in 539 BCE?
why: It records Cyrus's version of the conquest and policies toward subject peoples. It is often described as an early statement of religious tolerance, though scholars debate that reading.
extra: It is held in the British Museum.

q: Ancient DNA (2021) showed that the earliest Tarim Basin mummies derived from:
opts: A distinct local lineage descended from Ancient North Eurasians
ans: A distinct local lineage descended from Ancient North Eurasians
why: The study found they were genetically isolated and not recent migrants from the steppe. Their culture borrowed from neighbours, such as cheese-making and wheat.
extra: The mummies were found in Xinjiang.

q: Pavlopetri, off southern Greece, is often called:
opts: The oldest known submerged town with a planned layout
ans: The oldest known submerged town with a planned layout
why: The Bronze Age town dates back to about 3000 BCE and has streets, buildings and tombs under shallow water. It was surveyed in detail in 2009.
extra: It lies in Laconia.

q: The durability of Roman concrete is largely attributed to the use of:
why: Pozzolanic reactions produce hardy binding compounds, especially in seawater. Studies in 2023 highlighted lime clasts that may help the material self-heal.
extra: The Pantheon's dome remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

q: Sanxingdui in Sichuan, where large bronze masks and a tall bronze figure were found, belongs to which ancient culture?
opts: Shu culture of the Bronze Age
ans: Shu culture of the Bronze Age
why: Discoveries in 1986 revealed a sophisticated society with a distinct artistic tradition that differs from the Shang heartland. Its pits contained bronzes, jade and ivory.
extra: Its writing system, if any, is unknown.

q: Genome analysis of Ötzi, the Iceman found in 1991, revealed the oldest known case of which infection?
why: Researchers detected Borrelia DNA in his remains. He also carried Helicobacter pylori and had worn tattoos.
extra: He died about 5,300 years ago in the Alps and was carrying a copper axe.

q: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved from a single rock by working:
why: Craftsmen sculpted it from a basalt cliff in the 8th century under the Rashtrakutas. About 200,000 tonnes of rock are thought to have been removed.
extra: It is Cave 16 at Ellora.

q: The Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (Oxus Civilisation) flourished in which region?
why: BMAC towns existed from about 2300 to 1700 BCE in what is now Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Afghanistan. They had trade contacts with the Indus and Iran.
extra: Fortified oasis settlements and elaborate metalwork characterise it.

q: In 1924 Raymond Dart described the Taung Child, the first australopithecine fossil, found in which country?
why: Dart named it Australopithecus africanus and argued that it was a human ancestor. The idea was resisted for decades, partly because Piltdown seemed to suggest a large brain came first.
extra: The Taung skull was probably killed by an eagle, according to later studies.

q: Which Namib Desert plant has only two strap-like leaves that grow continuously from the base, and some individuals live over a thousand years?
why: Welwitschia lives in a fog-fed desert and absorbs moisture through its leaves; the leaf tips fray and wear away as the base keeps growing. It is the only living species in its genus and family.
extra: It was named after Friedrich Welwitsch, who found it in Angola in 1859.

q: The 'Dancing Girl' statuette of Mohenjo-daro was made using:
why: A wax model is covered in clay, and then melted out and replaced by molten bronze. The technique was well established in the Indus cities.
extra: The statuette is about 10 cm tall and dates to roughly 2500 BCE.

q: In which year did the last known thylacine die in captivity at Hobart Zoo?
why: The last known captive animal died in September 1936. The Tasmanian tiger was hunted and lost habitat under a bounty scheme.
extra: It looked like a wolf but was a marsupial, a classic case of convergent evolution.

q: In the Samudra Manthan (churning of the ocean), which serpent served as the churning rope?
why: Devas and asuras used Mount Mandara as the churning rod and Vasuki as the rope. Vishnu supported the mountain as the tortoise avatar Kurma.
extra: The churning produced amrita, the nectar of immortality, and also the poison halahala, swallowed by Shiva.

q: Which of these animals is endemic to the Western Ghats?
why: The Nilgiri tahr (Nilgiritragus hylocrius) lives on the high grassy slopes of the southern Western Ghats. The Himalayan tahr is a different species of the Himalaya.
extra: It is the state animal of Tamil Nadu, and Eravikulam National Park is a stronghold.

q: Engraved ochre pieces from Blombos Cave in South Africa, about 75,000 years old, are important as evidence of:
why: The cross-hatched designs suggest abstract representation. The cave also yielded shell beads and an ochre-processing workshop.
extra: The finds show that symbolic thinking existed in Africa long before Europe's cave art.

q: In Irish mythology, the Tuatha De Danann retreat into mounds after being defeated by whom?
why: The Milesians, ancestors of the Gaels, took Ireland and the Tuatha De Danann went underground into the sidhe. They are often seen as the origin of the fairy folk.
extra: The tale is recorded in the Lebor Gabala Erenn.

q: The Phaistos Disc from Crete is famous because:
opts: It is the oldest known map
Its stamped symbols have never been deciphered
It is a forgery proven in 1950
It is written in Linear B
ans: Its stamped symbols have never been deciphered
why: The clay disc bears spiral text made using individual stamps. It was found in 1908 by Luigi Pernier and may be an early example of movable type.
extra: Only a single example exists.

q: Tardigrades survive extreme drying by entering a state in which metabolism falls to almost undetectable levels. What is this state called?
why: In cryptobiosis the animal expels most of its body water, curls into a 'tun' and suspends metabolism. Protective molecules, including tardigrade-specific disordered proteins, help preserve cell structures until water returns.
extra: Tardigrades were exposed to open space on the 2007 FOTON-M3 mission and some survived.

q: Phytoliths recovered from archaeological soils are:
opts: Microscopic silica bodies from plants that identify crops
ans: Microscopic silica bodies from plants that identify crops
why: Plants deposit silica in their cells, and the shapes are diagnostic of species. They persist in soils and on tools where other plant remains vanish.
extra: They have been used to trace rice and millet cultivation.

q: The bulbous knob at the snout tip of adult male gharials, used in vocal buzzing and display, is called the:
why: The ghara (named after an Indian clay pot) is present only in adult males of Gavialis gangeticus. It resonates during buzzing sounds and likely signals maturity to females.
extra: Gharials, specialised fish-eaters of North Indian rivers, are critically endangered.

q: The Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, emphasises:
opts: Wu wei, or effortless action in harmony with the Dao
ans: Wu wei, or effortless action in harmony with the Dao
why: It teaches simplicity, humility and aligning with nature. Its authorship and date are debated.
extra: Zhuangzi expanded Daoist thought with parables.

q: Which pre-Inca civilisation near Lake Titicaca built the Akapana pyramid and the Gateway of the Sun?
why: Tiwanaku flourished between about 500 and 1000 CE and used raised-field agriculture. It was a major religious and political centre in the Andes.
extra: It is located in modern Bolivia.

q: When attacked, hagfish produce a defensive slime whose strength comes from:
opts: Thousands of coiled protein threads that unravel in seawater
ans: Thousands of coiled protein threads that unravel in seawater
why: Hagfish glands release mucus along with coiled threads that uncoil and tangle in seawater, forming a cohesive slime that clogs the gills of predators. The threads are proteins, not silica or chitin.
extra: Hagfish are jawless fishes and can tie themselves in knots to remove slime from their own bodies.

q: The Brihadisvara Temple in Thanjavur was built by:
why: Completed around 1010 CE, it features a granite vimana about 66 metres high. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
extra: The temple's capstone is said to weigh around 80 tonnes.

q: Arthropleura, the giant millipede-like arthropod, lived during which period?
why: Arthropleura could exceed two metres in length and lived in coal-forming forests. Its tracks and body fossils are known from Europe and North America.
extra: Carboniferous oxygen levels were unusually high.

q: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Greek shipwreck, is best described as:
opts: An ancient analogue device for predicting astronomical events
ans: An ancient analogue device for predicting astronomical events
why: This geared bronze device, dated to roughly the 2nd to 1st century BCE, modelled the movements of the Sun, Moon and probably planets. It predicted eclipses using the Saros cycle.
extra: Sponge divers found the wreck in 1900.

q: Axolotls keep larval features such as external gills throughout adult life. This phenomenon is called:
why: Neoteny (a form of paedomorphosis) means juvenile traits are retained in the sexually mature animal. Axolotls rarely metamorphose unless exposed to thyroid hormone.
extra: Axolotls are famed for regenerating limbs, parts of the heart and even portions of the brain.

q: The Piltdown hoax, exposed in 1953, combined a human cranium with the jaw of:
why: Fluorine testing and anatomical analysis revealed the fraud. It had misled science for decades by supporting the idea that large brains evolved first.
extra: The forger remains unidentified.

q: Which 1565 battle led to the sack of Vijayanagara?
why: A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara's army and plundered the capital. Hampi never recovered.
extra: Hampi is a UNESCO site with extensive ruins.

q: At Catalhoyuk in Anatolia, most houses were entered through:
why: Houses were packed together without streets, and people moved across the roofs. James Mellaart began excavations in 1958, followed by Ian Hodder.
extra: The site dates to about 7100 to 5700 BCE.

q: How were the Nazca geoglyphs mostly made?
opts: By removing dark surface stones to expose lighter ground
ans: By removing dark surface stones to expose lighter ground
why: The Nazca culture (about 500 BCE to 500 CE) made lines and figures in the Peruvian desert. The dry climate has preserved them.
extra: AI-assisted surveys have identified many new figures.

q: Tiktaalik roseae is significant because it:
opts: Is a transitional form between reptiles and birds
Shows features intermediate between lobe-finned fish and early tetrapods
ans: Shows features intermediate between lobe-finned fish and early tetrapods
why: Tiktaalik, about 375 million years old, had a flat head, neck, robust fin bones and ribs while retaining gills and scales. It was found on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic.
extra: Its discoverers predicted the rock age and region where such a fossil should occur before searching.

q: William Rathje's Garbage Project applied archaeological methods to:
why: Rathje studied refuse in the United States starting in the 1970s. He found that what people say they consume differs from what they throw away.
extra: It founded the field sometimes called garbology.

q: Cahokia, whose largest earthwork is Monks Mound, was a major centre of which culture?
why: Cahokia peaked around 1050 to 1200 CE near modern St. Louis. It had plazas, mounds and a population possibly in the tens of thousands.
extra: Monks Mound is the largest earthen mound in North America.

q: Which Inca ruler is traditionally credited with building Machu Picchu as a royal estate?
why: The site dates to the mid-15th century and was abandoned around the Spanish conquest. Hiram Bingham brought it to international attention in 1911.
extra: Pachacuti expanded the Inca state dramatically.

q: Nan Madol, an ancient city of artificial islets built of basalt, lies off which Micronesian island?
why: Built from about the 12th century, it was the seat of the Saudeleur dynasty. Massive prismatic basalt logs were stacked to form walls.
extra: It is sometimes called the 'Venice of the Pacific'.

q: The Prayag Prashasti, inscribed on the Allahabad pillar, praises which Gupta ruler?
why: It was composed by the court poet Harishena and records Samudragupta's conquests. It lists kings and tribes across the subcontinent.
extra: The pillar also bears Ashokan edicts.

q: In 2016, researchers reported that many lichens contain a third symbiotic partner. What is it?
why: Lichens were long thought to be a partnership of one fungus and one alga or cyanobacterium. Spribille and colleagues found yeasts embedded in the cortex of many macrolichens, challenging that two-partner model.
extra: Slow-growing crustose lichens are used to date rock surfaces in a method called lichenometry.

q: In the Rigveda, Indra's most famous deed is slaying:
why: Vritra, a serpentine being, had blocked the rivers, and Indra's thunderbolt freed them. The myth has Indo-European parallels.
extra: Ravana, Hiranyakashipu and Mahishasura appear in later epic and Puranic texts.

q: Archaeological work at Jwalapuram in southern India has been used to argue that the Toba ash did NOT:
opts: Cause a severe collapse of human populations
ans: Cause a severe collapse of human populations
why: Stone tool assemblages above and below the ash layer showed continuity of technology. This suggests that populations survived the event.
extra: The site's interpretation as showing early modern humans in India is debated.

q: In which year was the cheetah officially declared extinct in India?
why: Hunting, habitat loss and prey decline contributed to the loss of the Asiatic cheetah in India. The last confirmed individuals are recorded from central India in the 1940s.
extra: In 2022 cheetahs from Namibia were translocated to Kuno National Park.

q: The Linear B tablets, deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, record which language?
why: Linear B was used for palace accounts at Knossos, Pylos and other sites. Ventris's decipherment built on earlier analytical work by Alice Kober.
extra: Linear A, used by the Minoans, remains undeciphered.

q: Flinders Petrie's technique of sequence dating, used on predynastic graves, relied on:
opts: Ordering graves by changes in pottery styles
ans: Ordering graves by changes in pottery styles
why: Petrie arranged grave groups so that pottery types changed gradually over time. This is an early form of seriation.
extra: It allowed a relative chronology before radiometric methods.

q: The Vetala (Baital) tales, with King Vikrama and a spirit in a corpse, appear in the Kathasaritsagara compiled by Somadeva in which region?
why: Somadeva compiled the 11th-century Sanskrit collection for a queen of Kashmir. It is based on the lost Brihatkatha.
extra: Its frame stories influenced later collections.

q: Amazonian 'terra preta' soils are:
opts: Dark, fertile anthropogenic soils enriched with charcoal and waste
ans: Dark, fertile anthropogenic soils enriched with charcoal and waste
why: Pre-Columbian communities created them over centuries. They indicate large, managed settlements in the Amazon.
extra: They retain fertility, unlike most tropical soils.

q: Which biogeographic boundary, running between Bali and Lombok, separates predominantly Asian fauna from Australasian fauna?
why: Alfred Russel Wallace noticed that birds and mammals of Bali differ sharply from those only a short distance away on Lombok. A deep strait kept the two faunas apart even when Ice Age sea levels were low.
extra: The transitional zone between Asian and Australian faunas is known as Wallacea.

q: Tools from Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu were dated to about 385,000 years ago and indicate:
opts: Middle Palaeolithic technology in India far earlier than expected
ans: Middle Palaeolithic technology in India far earlier than expected
why: The 2018 study found Levallois-type tools, which appear at similar times to Africa and Europe. This challenged ideas that such technology arrived late with modern humans.
extra: The site lies near Chennai.

q: The extinct giraffid Sivatherium was first described from fossils in which Indian region?
why: Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley described it in the 1830s. The name means 'Shiva's beast' in reference to the Hindu deity.
extra: It was a heavily built relative of the giraffe and okapi.

q: Adi Shankara is associated with which philosophical school?
why: Advaita holds that the individual self and Brahman are identical. Shankara wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, Gita and Brahma Sutras.
extra: He is traditionally dated to the 8th century CE.

q: The John Frum movement in Vanuatu is a classic example of a:
why: Such movements arose after contact with Western goods and wartime supply flows. Followers hoped ritual would bring wealth and a new order.
extra: The movement persists, with annual celebrations.

q: Which mammal is classified as eusocial, with a single breeding queen and non-breeding workers?
why: Naked mole-rats live in underground colonies in East Africa where one queen and a few males breed while the rest dig, forage and defend. Meerkats breed cooperatively but lack this strict reproductive caste system.
extra: Naked mole-rats are unusually long-lived for rodents of their size and resistant to low oxygen.

q: In the Shatapatha Brahmana, which incarnation warns Manu of a coming flood?
why: Manu saves a small fish that grows to enormous size and warns him to build a boat. The fish later tows the boat to safety.
extra: Later Puranic texts identify the fish as the avatar of Vishnu.

q: Which of these was a 'founder crop' of Neolithic Southwest Asia?
why: The founder crops included emmer, einkorn, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. They were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000 years ago.
extra: Maize, potato and quinoa were domesticated in the Americas.

q: Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was commissioned by which ruler in 1443?
why: Sejong and scholars designed a phonetic script to be learned easily by commoners. Its letters reflect the shape of the mouth in producing sounds.
extra: Korea celebrates Hangul Day in October.

q: The 'Snowball Earth' glaciations occurred during which period?
why: The Cryogenian (about 720 to 635 million years ago) saw ice sheets that may have reached the tropics. Complex animals appear in the fossil record soon after.
extra: Evidence includes glacial deposits found on rocks that were near the equator at the time.

q: Mangrove trees such as those of the Sundarbans have upward-growing roots called pneumatophores. What is their main function?
opts: Taking in oxygen in waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud
ans: Taking in oxygen in waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud
why: Waterlogged mud is low in oxygen, so pneumatophores poke above the surface and exchange gases through pores called lenticels. Mangroves also use other adaptations such as salt excretion and viviparous seedlings.
extra: The Sundarbans, shared by India and Bangladesh, is the largest contiguous mangrove forest in the world.

q: The Jataka tales narrate:
opts: Previous births of the Buddha as a bodhisattva
The spread of Buddhism in Sri Lanka
ans: Previous births of the Buddha as a bodhisattva
why: There are 547 tales in the Pali collection, often involving animals. They teach moral lessons and appear in art at sites like Sanchi and Bharhut.
extra: Some tales have parallels in Aesop's fables.

q: Fossils of ichthyosaurs with embryos inside the body show that they were:
opts: Egg-layers that buried eggs in sand
why: Some specimens preserve fetuses in the birth canal or newborns just emerging, tail first. This suggests that live birth was a necessary adaptation for fully marine reptiles.
extra: Ichthyosaurs evolved a streamlined, dolphin-like body from land reptile ancestors.

q: Which East African kingdom, centred in the Ethiopian highlands, minted its own coins and adopted Christianity under King Ezana in the 4th century?
why: Aksum controlled Red Sea trade and was one of the major powers of its age. Its monumental stelae mark royal burials.
extra: Aksumite coins bear Greek legends and Christian crosses after Ezana.

q: The Pax6 gene is evolutionarily significant because:
opts: It helps trigger eye development in animals as different as flies and mammals
ans: It helps trigger eye development in animals as different as flies and mammals
why: Pax6 homologues are used in eye development across animals, suggesting deep shared genetic machinery. Expressing a mouse Pax6 gene in fly tissues can cause ectopic eyes with fly structure.
extra: The finding challenged older ideas that eyes evolved fully independently many times.

q: Which kingdom is credited with some of the earliest coins made of electrum, around 600 BCE?
why: Lydian electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, was stamped with lion designs. King Croesus later introduced coins of pure gold and silver.
extra: Coinage spread quickly through Greek cities.

q: Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) is notable for formalising:
opts: Rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers
ans: Rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers
why: He gave rules for operations with positive and negative quantities and zero, though his treatment of division by zero was flawed. His work reached the Arab world.
extra: He also gave a formula for the area of cyclic quadrilaterals.

q: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 is famous for:
opts: His distribution of gold, which affected gold values in Cairo
Opening the sea route to India
ans: His distribution of gold, which affected gold values in Cairo
why: The ruler of the Mali Empire travelled with a huge entourage and gave away gold. Accounts say it depressed the gold price for years.
extra: Timbuktu became a major centre of Islamic scholarship under Mali.

q: Which Iranian-speaking people were the principal merchants of the early Silk Road?
why: Based in Samarkand and Bukhara, Sogdians ran caravans between China and the West. Their language was widely used for trade.
extra: The 'Sogdian Ancient Letters' of about 313 CE record their trade networks.

q: Which 53 BCE battle saw the Roman general Crassus killed and legionary standards lost to the Parthians?
why: Parthian horse archers and cataphracts crushed the Roman army. It was a famous Roman defeat.
extra: The standards were returned to Augustus in 20 BCE.

q: Hox genes are important in animal evolution because they:
opts: Specify identity of body regions along the head-to-tail axis
ans: Specify identity of body regions along the head-to-tail axis
why: Hox genes are arranged in clusters and expressed in sequence along the body axis. Changes in their expression can alter segment identity.
extra: Remarkably similar Hox clusters occur in flies and mammals.

q: Wootz steel, celebrated for its patterned blades, originated in:
why: Wootz was produced by heating iron and carbon in sealed crucibles. It was exported to the Middle East, where it became the basis for pattern-welded Damascus blades.
extra: The word 'wootz' may derive from the Kannada or Telugu term 'ukku'.

q: The oldest known surviving law code, predating Hammurabi's, is attributed to:
why: Dated to about 2100 to 2050 BCE, the code uses fines rather than the physical retaliation seen in later codes. It was written in Sumerian.
extra: Hammurabi's code dates to about 1754 BCE.

q: Who rediscovered the manuscript of the Arthashastra in 1905?
why: Shamasastry found the palm-leaf manuscript in Mysore and published it soon after. The text on statecraft is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya).
extra: Its modern form likely incorporates layers from several centuries.

q: Which Aztec deity of sun and war was patron of Tenochtitlan?
why: His twin shrine with Tlaloc crowned the Templo Mayor. Aztec tradition said Huitzilopochtli led the Mexica to found their city.
extra: The temple's remains lie beneath central Mexico City.

q: The Eleusinian Mysteries honoured which deities?
why: Initiates took part in secret rites at Eleusis that promised a better afterlife. The rites ran for nearly two thousand years.
extra: Participants swore not to reveal the secrets.

q: The Popol Vuh is a sacred narrative of which Maya people?
why: It tells of the creation of humans from maize and of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, who defeat the lords of Xibalba. A colonial-era manuscript preserved it.
extra: Friar Francisco Ximenez copied and translated it in the early 18th century.

q: Carthage was founded, according to tradition, as a colony of which Phoenician city?
why: Tradition places the foundation around 814 BCE under Queen Dido (Elissa). Carthage grew into a Mediterranean power rivalling Rome.
extra: The Phoenician alphabet influenced Greek and then Latin scripts.

q: Our division of the hour into 60 minutes ultimately traces back to the number system of:
why: Mesopotamian scribes used a base-60 (sexagesimal) system for counting and astronomy. It survives in time and angle measurement.
extra: Base 60 is convenient because 60 has many divisors.

q: Which Pythagorean belief resembles Indian ideas of rebirth?
opts: Belief in the music of the spheres
why: Pythagoreans taught that souls pass into new bodies. They also practised dietary restrictions.
extra: Pythagoras is said to have recognised a dead friend's soul in a dog.

q: Indohyus, a small fossil mammal from Kashmir, is important because it:
opts: Is the ancestor of all ruminants
Is a close relative of whales and shows early aquatic adaptations
ans: Is a close relative of whales and shows early aquatic adaptations
why: Indohyus was a raccoon-sized artiodactyl with dense bones that suggest wading behaviour. A 2007 study placed it close to cetaceans, supporting whale origins from land mammals near Indo-Pakistan.
extra: Pakicetus, another early relative, was found in Pakistan.

q: The central icon in Roman Mithraic temples shows Mithras:
why: This tauroctony adorns the underground temples called mithraea. Mithraism was a mystery cult popular among Roman soldiers.
extra: Only men were admitted.

q: Helicoprion, a Permian fish with a spiral tooth whorl, is most closely related to:
why: CT scans of a specimen in 2013 indicated that the whorl sat in the lower jaw and that Helicoprion was a chondrichthyan nested within the chimaera lineage. Earlier artists put the whorl on the snout or dorsal fin.
extra: Its remains are known from Idaho, Russia and elsewhere.

q: The Ajanta caves were brought to wider attention in 1819 by:
opts: A British officer, John Smith, on a hunting trip
ans: A British officer, John Smith, on a hunting trip
why: Smith of the Madras Army saw the horseshoe-shaped gorge and found the painted caves. The murals are an outstanding example of Buddhist art.
extra: The caves date from the 2nd century BCE to about 480 CE.

q: Stoicism takes its name from the Stoa Poikile in Athens and was founded by:
why: Zeno taught around 300 BCE and stressed living in accordance with nature and reason. The school influenced Roman thinkers such as Seneca and Marcus Aurelius.
extra: Zeno came from Cyprus.

q: The decline of Indus cities after c. 1900 BCE is most commonly linked to:
why: Climate and river changes disrupted agriculture and trade, and populations dispersed gradually. Studies of the Ghaggar-Hakra system suggest that rivers dried or moved.
extra: The 4.2-kiloyear drought event may have also contributed.

q: Which technology enabled ancient China to produce cast iron centuries before Europe?
why: Chinese metalworkers developed high-temperature furnaces and cast iron by the 5th century BCE. The ability to pour iron allowed mass production of tools.
extra: Europe used cast iron widely only in the late medieval period.

q: Taphonomy is the study of:
opts: Rates of mutation in ancient DNA
Processes affecting remains between death and fossilisation
ans: Processes affecting remains between death and fossilisation
why: Taphonomy examines decay, scavenging, transport, burial and chemical change. It helps scientists judge how complete or biased a fossil record is.
extra: The term was coined by Ivan Efremov in 1940.

q: Adult lactase persistence arose independently in European and African pastoralist populations. This is an example of:
why: Cultures that relied on dairying favoured mutations that keep lactase active into adulthood. Different mutations became common in different regions.
extra: Most of the world's adults are lactose intolerant to some degree.

q: Which dating method is suited to volcanic ash layers at Olduvai Gorge that are more than 100,000 years old?
why: These methods measure radioactive decay of potassium-40 into argon in volcanic minerals. They date rocks that bracket the fossil-bearing layers.
extra: The technique helped date early hominin sites in East Africa.

q: Roughly 80 percent or more of land plants form which kind of partnership with fungi in their roots?
why: Mycorrhizal fungi extend the root system and supply phosphorus and nitrogen in exchange for plant sugars. Rhizobial nodules involve bacteria, not fungi, and lichens are partnerships with algae or cyanobacteria.
extra: Fossils from the roughly 407-million-year-old Rhynie chert show fungal associations in some of the earliest land plants.

q: Which of these was not one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions?
why: The Big Five are the end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic and end-Cretaceous events. There was no comparable mass extinction in the Middle Jurassic.
extra: The end-Permian event was the most severe.

q: What is the Thai version of the Ramayana called?
why: The Ramakien is a national epic of Thailand, preserved in several royal versions. The name Ayutthaya recalls Ayodhya.
extra: Hanuman and Thotsakan (Ravana) are popular figures in Thai drama.

q: The Etruscan language is notable because it is:
opts: Not part of the Indo-European family
ans: Not part of the Indo-European family
why: Etruscan is known from inscriptions in an alphabet adapted from Greek. It appears related to Raetic and Lemnian rather than to neighbouring Italic languages.
extra: Many Roman religious and civic practices were adopted from Etruscans.

q: The name 'Teotihuacan', meaning roughly 'place where the gods were created', was given by:
why: The original builders' name for the city is unknown. The Aztecs found the vast ruins centuries after its decline and regarded it as sacred.
extra: The city had pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead.

q: What does Leigh Van Valen's 'Red Queen hypothesis' propose?
opts: Species must keep evolving just to maintain fitness against coevolving species
ans: Species must keep evolving just to maintain fitness against coevolving species
why: In a world of competitors, predators and parasites, adaptation by one species puts pressure on others. The name borrows from Lewis Carroll's Red Queen who must run to stay in place.
extra: It is used to explain why sexual reproduction persists despite its costs.

q: In Jainism, the doctrine of anekantavada states that:
opts: The world has no beginning or end
Reality has many aspects, so truth is seen from multiple viewpoints
ans: Reality has many aspects, so truth is seen from multiple viewpoints
why: It underlies the parable of blind men and the elephant. The principle supports non-absolutism and tolerance.
extra: Mahavira is regarded as the 24th Tirthankara.

q: The Mongol 'yam' was a:
opts: Relay system of posting stations for messengers
ans: Relay system of posting stations for messengers
why: Riders carrying official passports (paiza) changed horses at stations along main routes. It allowed fast communication across vast territories.
extra: The security under Mongol rule is called the Pax Mongolica.

q: Which pharaoh promoted worship of the Aten and founded a new capital at Akhetaten?
why: He shifted state religion away from Amun and built Akhetaten (modern Amarna). His successors restored the old gods.
extra: Tutankhamun was probably his son.

q: The 'dancing plague' of 1518 occurred in which city?
why: Dozens or hundreds of people reportedly danced for days. Explanations include mass psychogenic illness, while the ergot hypothesis has been questioned.
extra: Authorities even hired musicians in an attempt to cure it.

q: True or false: the passenger pigeon was once among the most abundant birds on Earth, with a population in the billions.
why: Flocks of passenger pigeons darkened the sky in 19th-century North America. Commercial hunting and habitat loss then caused a collapse within decades.
extra: The last individual, Martha, died at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914.

q: The golden rhinoceros was found at Mapungubwe, in which country?
why: Mapungubwe was a trading state from about 1075 to 1220 CE in the Limpopo valley. It exchanged gold and ivory for Indian Ocean goods.
extra: It was a precursor to Great Zimbabwe.

q: The 4.2-kiloyear aridification event is linked to the collapse of which Mesopotamian empire?
why: Evidence from Tell Leilan suggests abandonment during a severe drought. The event may also have affected Egypt and the Indus region.
extra: Akkad was founded by Sargon.

q: Which bird makes the longest known annual migration, travelling roughly pole to pole?
why: Arctic terns breed in the Arctic and winter around Antarctic waters, with tracked birds covering about 70,000 km in a year. The bar-tailed godwit holds the record for longest non-stop flight, not the longest annual route.
extra: Because they live in near-constant daylight at both ends, Arctic terns experience more daylight than any other animal.

q: The coconut crab, Birgus latro, is notable as:
opts: The only crab that can fly
why: Coconut crabs are huge terrestrial hermit-crab relatives of Indo-Pacific islands. Juveniles use discarded shells, but adults develop a hardened abdomen and no longer carry shells.
extra: Adults can open coconuts and are known to carry off objects such as cutlery, according to island accounts.

q: Which voyaging canoe, in 1976, sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments to demonstrate traditional Polynesian navigation?
why: The voyage used stars, swells and bird behaviour, guided by Micronesian master navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal. It sparked a revival of traditional wayfinding.
extra: Kon-Tiki was a 1947 raft expedition.

q: Ashoka's son Mahinda is traditionally credited with introducing Buddhism to:
why: He travelled to Sri Lanka and converted King Devanampiya Tissa. A sapling of the Bodhi tree was brought by Sanghamitta.
extra: The Mahavamsa chronicles these events.

q: The potlatch is a ceremonial feast and gift-giving system among Indigenous peoples of:
opts: The Pacific Northwest coast of North America
ans: The Pacific Northwest coast of North America
why: Hosts distribute wealth to display rank and validate claims. Canada banned potlatches from 1885 to 1951.
extra: Totem poles and masks are linked to these ceremonies.

q: In Richard Lenski's long-term experiment, which novel trait emerged in one E. coli population after about 31,000 generations?
opts: Ability to use citrate in the presence of oxygen
ans: Ability to use citrate in the presence of oxygen
why: One of twelve lines evolved the ability to use citrate, a medium component that E. coli normally cannot use aerobically. Replaying earlier frozen populations showed that earlier mutations had made this possible.
extra: The experiment began in 1988 and has run for tens of thousands of generations.

q: The wooden throwing spears of Schoningen, Germany, about 300,000 years old, are attributed to:
opts: Early Neanderthal-lineage or Homo heidelbergensis hunters
ans: Early Neanderthal-lineage or Homo heidelbergensis hunters
why: The well-balanced spears and butchered horses show organised hunting long before modern humans reached Europe. Waterlogged conditions preserved the wood.
extra: Their balance resembles that of modern javelins.

q: In the fig and fig wasp mutualism, where do the wasp larvae develop?
opts: In the flowers of neighbouring plants
Under the bark of the tree
In the soil beneath the tree
why: Female wasps squeeze through the tiny ostiole of a fig, pollinate the internal flowers and lay eggs in some ovules. Larvae develop in those ovules, and the new generation mates inside before dispersing.
extra: A fig is an inverted inflorescence, not a conventional fruit.

q: The saying 'Tat tvam asi' ('That thou art') appears in which Upanishad?
why: Uddalaka Aruni teaches his son Shvetaketu that the self is identical with ultimate reality. It is one of the Mahavakyas.
extra: It is one of the oldest Upanishads.

q: In the Milinda Panha, the Indo-Greek king Menander I debates which Buddhist monk?
why: The text records questions on the nature of self and rebirth. Menander ruled in northwestern India in the 2nd century BCE.
extra: The debate is preserved in Pali.

q: How were the Sulawesi cave paintings dated to over 45,000 years old?
opts: Uranium-series dating of calcite crusts that formed over the paint
ans: Uranium-series dating of calcite crusts that formed over the paint
why: Minimum ages are obtained from the calcium carbonate layers that grew over the art. This showed that figurative art existed in Southeast Asia as early as in Europe.
extra: One painting is of a Sulawesi warty pig.

q: Evidence of early dentistry, with drilled molars about 9,000 years ago, has been reported from which Neolithic site?
why: Drilling in tooth crowns using flint tools was found in several individuals at Mehrgarh in present-day Pakistan. Some teeth show signs of healing.
extra: Mehrgarh is regarded as a precursor to Indus Valley settlement.

q: The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 (c. 1800 BCE) is widely interpreted as listing:
why: The tablet's numbers form sets of integers fitting a^2 + b^2 = c^2. Whether it was a teaching aid or a table of solutions is debated.
extra: It predates Pythagoras by over a thousand years.

q: Bdelloid rotifers are notable evolutionarily because they:
opts: Are older than all other animals
Appear to have reproduced asexually for tens of millions of years
ans: Appear to have reproduced asexually for tens of millions of years
why: No males or meiosis are known in this group, yet they diversified into hundreds of species. They resist desiccation and radiation damage and take up foreign DNA.
extra: They have been called an 'evolutionary scandal'.

q: Budj Bim in Victoria, Australia, is recognised for ancient aquaculture of:
why: Channels, weirs and ponds in a volcanic landscape trapped and farmed short-finned eels. The system is thousands of years old.
extra: It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

q: Which two Southeast Asian countries use the Garuda in their national emblems?
why: Garuda, the eagle-like vehicle of Vishnu, appears in both emblems. Indonesia's national airline is named after it.
extra: The Thai version is called Phra Khrut Pha.

q: In 1984 DNA from which extinct animal became the first to be sequenced?
why: Russell Higuchi and colleagues extracted short sequences from a museum skin of this zebra-like animal. Later work showed it was a subspecies of the plains zebra.
extra: The Quagga Project in South Africa breeds zebras to recreate its appearance.

q: Which Rigvedic hymn (10.129) famously doubts whether even the highest overseer knows how the universe came into being?
why: The hymn describes a time before existence and non-existence and ends with a question about whether the creator knows. It is celebrated for its philosophical scepticism.
extra: The Purusha Sukta, by contrast, describes creation from a cosmic being.

q: Doggerland was:
opts: A land area in the North Sea submerged after the last Ice Age
ans: A land area in the North Sea submerged after the last Ice Age
why: Rising sea level flooded the land between Britain and continental Europe. Mammoth tusks and tools have been trawled up from the seabed.
extra: A tsunami around 6200 BCE (Storegga) hit its remnants.

q: Which application of the wheel appears to have preceded wheeled transport?
why: Evidence for turntables and potter's wheels appears in Mesopotamia in the mid-4th millennium BCE or earlier. Wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 to 3000 BCE across Europe and the Near East.
extra: The wheel and axle may have emerged from mining technology.

q: Large-scale distillation of metallic zinc was pioneered by medieval metallurgists at:
why: Retort furnaces at Zawar produced zinc by about the 12th to 13th centuries. Europe did not produce zinc on a similar scale until the 18th century.
extra: Zinc is hard to smelt because it vaporises at high temperatures.

q: The Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics, founded by Madhava of Sangamagrama, discovered:
opts: Infinite series for trigonometric functions and pi
ans: Infinite series for trigonometric functions and pi
why: Madhava's series for sine, cosine and arctangent predate their European rediscovery by centuries. The school flourished in the 14th to 16th centuries.
extra: The Nilakantha Somayaji later refined models of planetary motion.

q: Thonis-Heracleion, a sunken Egyptian port city, was rediscovered in 2000 by:
why: The city lies in Abu Qir Bay and was submerged by earthquakes and rising water. Excavations revealed temples, statues and many ships.
extra: Thonis and Heracleion were once thought to be separate cities.

q: The Easter Island moai were mostly carved from compressed volcanic ash at which quarry?
why: The volcanic tuff was easy to carve, and hundreds of unfinished statues remain in the quarry. Many were then transported across the island.
extra: Some moai have buried torsos that are larger than the visible heads.

q: Pando, a quaking aspen colony in Utah, is notable as:
opts: A hybrid species of poplar and willow
The tallest tree in North America
A single genetic individual with thousands of stems
A forest planted in the 19th century
ans: A single genetic individual with thousands of stems
why: Pando consists of about 47,000 genetically identical stems linked by one root system. It is considered among the heaviest known organisms.
extra: Pando is declining in places because grazing animals browse young shoots.

q: The Finnish national epic Kalevala was compiled in 1835 by:
why: Lonnrot collected oral poetry from Karelian singers and shaped it into an epic. It shaped Finnish national identity.
extra: It influenced Tolkien's Silmarillion.

q: Marcel Mauss's The Gift argued that gift exchange:
opts: Creates reciprocal obligations and social bonds
ans: Creates reciprocal obligations and social bonds
why: Mauss showed that gifts in many societies carry an obligation to give, receive and reciprocate. This binds groups together.
extra: The idea influenced later work on reciprocity and exchange.

q: The Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago was driven by:
opts: Mass volcanism of the Deccan type
why: Cyanobacteria produced oxygen faster than it was consumed, so free oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere. Banded iron formations record oxidation of dissolved iron in earlier oceans.
extra: The event may have triggered the Huronian glaciation by oxidising methane.

q: The Ajivika school founded by Makkhali Gosala emphasised:
why: Ajivikas held that fate governs all and that actions do not change destiny. They were rivals of Buddhists and Jains.
extra: Ashoka dedicated the Barabar caves to Ajivika ascetics.

q: Aryabhata (born 476 CE) proposed that the apparent westward motion of stars is due to:
why: In the Aryabhatiya, he described a rotating Earth and gave accurate values for astronomical constants. He also approximated pi to four decimal places.
extra: India's first satellite was named after him.

q: Why are ammonites valuable to biostratigraphers?
opts: They evolved rapidly and were widespread, so they date and correlate rock layers
ans: They evolved rapidly and were widespread, so they date and correlate rock layers
why: Species with short time ranges and broad distributions make good index fossils. Ammonite zones allow Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks to be correlated across continents.
extra: Ammonites vanished at the end-Cretaceous, though their relative the nautilus survives.

q: The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in which three scripts or languages?
why: The parallel texts allowed scholars to compare Greek with Egyptian scripts. Champollion announced his breakthrough in 1822.
extra: French soldiers found it near Rashid in 1799.

q: Bog bodies such as Tollund Man are preserved by:
why: Sphagnum moss creates acidic conditions that tan the skin and slow decay. Tollund Man was found in Denmark in 1950 with a leather noose.
extra: He lived around the 4th century BCE.

q: The Toba super-eruption in Sumatra occurred about:
why: It was among the largest volcanic eruptions of the last few million years. Some scientists proposed it triggered a human population bottleneck, though this is disputed.
extra: Toba ash has been identified as far away as India.

q: Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance. What information does it convey?
opts: The presence of predators in the hive
Distance and direction of a food source relative to the sun
