ans: Distance and direction of a food source relative to the sun
why: The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical encodes direction relative to the sun, and the duration encodes distance. Recruits then fly out to the location.
extra: Von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.

q: Radiocarbon dating of the Bakhshali manuscript has been used to argue that it:
opts: Contains the earliest known written dot symbol for zero
ans: Contains the earliest known written dot symbol for zero
why: Oxford researchers found birch-bark layers dating from different centuries, with the earliest as old as the 3rd to 4th century CE. The manuscript uses a dot as a placeholder.
extra: It was found in 1881 near Bakhshali in present-day Pakistan.

q: The Hohle Fels Venus, around 35,000-40,000 years old, was found in which country?
why: This tiny figure was carved from mammoth ivory in the Swabian Jura. It is among the oldest known depictions of the human body.
extra: The same region yielded the Lion-man statue and early bone flutes.

q: Radiocarbon dating of the Voynich manuscript's parchment indicates it dates from:
why: The parchment dates to about 1404 to 1438. The text remains undeciphered.
extra: It is held at Yale's Beinecke Library.

q: Evidence of a ploughed field from the early Harappan phase was found at:
why: The Rajasthan site shows criss-cross furrows, suggesting a complex of cultivation. It also has fire altars.
extra: Its name means 'black bangles'.

q: When did the Cambrian explosion begin?
why: The Cambrian began about 539 million years ago and saw a rapid appearance of many animal body plans in the fossil record. Earlier animals existed, but hard shells and complex ecosystems appeared then.
extra: Ecological factors such as predation and oxygen levels are proposed drivers.

q: The Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian in the 6th century under Khosrow I by:
why: From Persian it passed to Arabic as Kalila wa Dimna and then to Europe. Its animal fables have parallels in folktales worldwide.
extra: The text is attributed to Vishnu Sharma.

q: The Harris matrix is used in archaeology to:
opts: Record the stratigraphic sequence of excavated contexts
ans: Record the stratigraphic sequence of excavated contexts
why: Edward Harris devised it in 1973 to show the relationships between layers and features. It helps archaeologists interpret the order of deposition.
extra: It was developed during work at Winchester.

q: Ancient DNA studies (2015) linked a major shift in European ancestry around 3000 BCE to migrations of:
why: Steppe-related ancestry spread across Europe with Corded Ware and later cultures. It is connected to debates on the spread of Indo-European languages.
extra: The Yamnaya culture lived north of the Black Sea.

q: The 'Axial Age' of Karl Jaspers refers to:
opts: The rise of monotheism in Egypt
Roughly 800-200 BCE, when major philosophical and religious traditions arose in several regions
ans: Roughly 800-200 BCE, when major philosophical and religious traditions arose in several regions
why: Jaspers observed that thinkers such as Confucius, the Buddha, Socrates and the Hebrew prophets emerged in separate regions. He argued that this was a turning point.
extra: The concept is debated by historians.

q: Egyptian blue, widely used from about 3000 BCE, is considered the earliest:
why: It is a calcium copper silicate made by heating sand, copper compounds and a calcium source. It was used on tombs, statues and mummy cases.
extra: It emits near-infrared light when excited, allowing detection of faded traces.

q: Why does a Venus flytrap not close on every raindrop?
opts: Closure needs two trigger-hair touches within about 20 seconds
Rain makes the leaf too slippery
Its trigger hairs only detect heat
ans: Closure needs two trigger-hair touches within about 20 seconds
why: Each hair deflection generates an electrical signal, and the trap only shuts when two signals occur within a short interval. This reduces the cost of false alarms.
extra: More touches from a struggling insect prompt tighter sealing and digestive enzyme production.

q: A feathered dinosaur tail preserved in amber, reported in 2016, came from which country?
why: The amber from the Hukawng Valley is about 99 million years old and enclosed a small coelurosaur tail with feathers. Burmese amber has also yielded birds, lizards and insects.
extra: The find confirmed feather structure in detail, including barbs and barbules.

q: In 1025 CE, which Chola ruler launched a naval expedition against Srivijaya?
why: The campaign struck Srivijaya's ports on the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, protecting Chola trade interests. It is a rare example of an Indian naval expedition abroad.
extra: He founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram.

q: The Benin Bronzes, looted by British forces in 1897, come from a kingdom in present-day:
why: The Kingdom of Benin, centred on the Edo people, produced brass plaques and sculptures for the royal court. They are now in museums worldwide.
extra: Repatriation has been the subject of discussions and agreements.

q: Rongorongo is an undeciphered glyph system from which island?
why: Wooden tablets carved with rows of glyphs survive in a few museums. Whether it is true writing is debated.
extra: Only about two dozen objects are known.

q: True or false: 'Mitochondrial Eve' was the only woman alive in her time.
why: Mitochondrial Eve is the most recent common ancestor of all living humans through the maternal line, living perhaps 150,000 to 200,000 years ago in Africa. Other women lived then, but their maternal lines died out.
extra: Y-chromosomal Adam is the paternal analogue and lived at a different time.

q: What word was found carved on a post when John White returned to Roanoke in 1590?
why: White found the colony abandoned with this single word. It probably referred to a nearby island and its inhabitants.
extra: The fate of the colonists remains unresolved.

q: Genetic studies identify the closest living relative of the extinct dodo as the:
why: DNA work in 2002 placed the dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire within a clade whose closest living relative is Caloenas nicobarica. The bird is found on islands including the Nicobars in India.
extra: The dodo went extinct on Mauritius in the late 17th century after human arrival.

q: Genetic and archaeological evidence indicates that the first domesticated animal was probably the:
why: Dogs descended from wolves and were domesticated before agriculture, probably more than 15,000 years ago. A burial at Bonn-Oberkassel, Germany, about 14,000 years old, included a dog.
extra: Sheep and goats followed with the Neolithic farming revolution.

q: What is the approximate half-life of carbon-14?
why: Radiocarbon dating compares remaining carbon-14 to expected levels in once-living material. It works effectively up to around 50,000 years.
extra: Willard Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960 for the method.

q: The Charvaka (Lokayata) school of Indian philosophy was notable for:
opts: Materialism that accepted only perception as valid knowledge
ans: Materialism that accepted only perception as valid knowledge
why: It rejected an afterlife and Vedic ritual authority. Much of what we know about it comes from its critics.
extra: It is among the heterodox (nastika) schools.

q: Which invention, spread from Asia into Europe, gave cavalry greater stability and shock power?
why: Stirrups gave riders support to use lances and swords more effectively. Evidence appears in China in the 4th century CE and spreads westwards in subsequent centuries.
extra: Some historians link stirrups to the development of medieval cavalry warfare.

q: In Samkhya philosophy, the two eternal realities are:
why: Purusha is pure consciousness and prakriti is material nature. Liberation comes from discriminating between them.
extra: Samkhya is one of the six orthodox schools.

q: Greek fire, a flammable weapon capable of burning on water, is associated with which empire?
why: Introduced in the 7th century, it was projected from ships through siphons. The composition remained a closely guarded secret.
extra: It helped defend Constantinople against Arab fleets.

q: In many Polynesian traditions, the demigod Maui is credited with:
opts: Fishing islands up from the sea and slowing the sun
ans: Fishing islands up from the sea and slowing the sun
why: Maui's hook is said to have pulled up islands such as Hawaii or New Zealand's North Island. He also snared the sun to lengthen the day.
extra: Versions differ widely across the Pacific.

q: 'Lucy', discovered in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, belongs to which species?
why: The roughly 3.2-million-year-old skeleton showed a mix of upright-walking pelvic anatomy and ape-like upper body and skull proportions. It showed that bipedalism preceded large brains.
extra: She was named after the Beatles song 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds'.

q: The Iron Age kingdom of Urartu was centred around which lake?
why: Urartu fortresses and irrigation canals dotted the Armenian Highlands from the 9th to 6th centuries BCE. It rivalled Assyria.
extra: The name Ararat is derived from Urartu.

q: What was the cargo of the Mary Celeste when she was found abandoned in 1872?
why: The brigantine was found drifting without her crew but with provisions intact. Theories include fear of an explosion of alcohol fumes.
extra: Several barrels were found empty.

q: Palaeontologists infer feather colour in fossils mainly by studying:
why: Melanosomes are pigment-bearing organelles whose shape correlates with colour, and they can be preserved in fossil feathers. Anchiornis was reconstructed in colour in 2010 using this method.
extra: Sinosauropteryx, a fossil from China, was inferred to have a banded reddish tail.

q: Which small Cretaceous dromaeosaurid had long feathers on both its forelimbs and hindlimbs?
why: Microraptor appears to have carried four wing-like surfaces and probably glided or flew short distances. It lived about 120 million years ago in China.
extra: Its feather structure suggests it could have been iridescent black.

q: The carved gateways (toranas) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi date to the period of which dynasty?
why: The stupa was founded under Ashoka and enlarged in the Sunga period, while the elaborate toranas were added in the 1st century BCE or so under the Satavahanas. They depict Jataka tales.
extra: Sanchi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Madhya Pradesh.

q: Which region holds more ancient pyramids than Egypt?
why: Rulers of the Kingdom of Kush built many steep-sided pyramids at sites such as Meroe and Nuri. Kushite kings also ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty.
extra: The Meroitic script has been read phonetically, but the language remains poorly understood.

q: Dimetrodon, the sail-backed Permian animal, is more closely related to which group?
why: Dimetrodon was a synapsid, part of the lineage leading to mammals. It lived about 295 to 272 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs.
extra: Its sail may have aided display or temperature regulation.

q: The treaty between Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Hattusili III (c. 1259 BCE) is often cited as:
opts: The first trade agreement of the Silk Road
The earliest surviving peace treaty between major powers
ans: The earliest surviving peace treaty between major powers
why: Versions survive in Egyptian hieroglyphs and in Akkadian cuneiform from Hattusa. It followed the Battle of Kadesh and set mutual defence and extradition terms.
extra: A copy is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York.

q: The Hymn to Ninkasi is a Sumerian poem honouring the goddess of:
why: It is also a recipe for brewing, describing steps like baking bread and mixing with sweet aromatics. It dates to about 1800 BCE.
extra: Beer was a staple in Mesopotamia.

q: Why was the name of Oviraptor ('egg thief') misleading?
opts: The eggs once thought stolen were later shown to be its own
ans: The eggs once thought stolen were later shown to be its own
why: In the 1920s a skeleton found above a nest was assumed to be raiding it. Later embryo-bearing eggs and brooding relatives like Citipati showed that the adult was sitting on its own clutch.
extra: Many oviraptorosaurs have been found in brooding postures.

q: Eldredge and Gould's 1972 theory of 'punctuated equilibrium' proposes that:
opts: Species often remain stable for long periods, with change concentrated in short bursts
ans: Species often remain stable for long periods, with change concentrated in short bursts
why: They argued that the fossil record's apparent gaps reflect how speciation commonly occurs in small, isolated populations. Stasis in the main lineage is the normal pattern.
extra: It stimulated debate on tempo and mode in evolution.

q: Which Roman legion, linked in popular accounts to Britain, vanishes from records in the 2nd century?
why: Its fate is uncertain. Evidence suggests it may have been reassigned elsewhere rather than annihilated.
extra: Stamped tiles of the legion have been found at Nijmegen.

q: Cai Lun, an official of the Han court, is traditionally credited with improving:
why: In 105 CE he presented a method using bark, rags and hemp. Archaeological finds suggest earlier paper existed.
extra: Paper reached the Islamic world by the 8th century.

q: Gigantopithecus blacki, the largest known ape, is most closely related to living:
why: Ancient proteins from a tooth found in Chuifeng Cave, China, placed it near the orangutan lineage. It stood roughly 2 to 3 metres tall.
extra: It probably went extinct about 300,000 years ago as forest habitats changed.

q: In 1909 Charles Walcott discovered which famous Cambrian fossil deposit in the Canadian Rockies?
why: Walcott found beautifully preserved soft-bodied animals in British Columbia that revealed the astonishing diversity of Cambrian life. The fauna is about 508 million years old.
extra: Walcott was later Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.

q: The archive of clay tablets found at Ebla in the 1970s comes from which modern country?
why: Excavations at Tell Mardikh uncovered thousands of tablets dating to about 2400 BCE. Many are written in the Eblaite language using Sumerian-derived cuneiform.
extra: Ebla was a major commercial power before its destruction.

q: Dickinsonia, a quilted flat organism, belongs to which fossil assemblage?
why: Dickinsonia lived in late Precambrian seas roughly 570 to 541 million years ago. Cholesterol-like biomarkers found in fossils have suggested an animal affinity, though the group remains debated.
extra: The Ediacara Hills of South Australia gave the biota its name, following Reg Sprigg's 1946 discoveries.

q: The 'Muziris papyrus' (2nd century CE) is a record of:
opts: A loan contract for a cargo shipment from Muziris to Alexandria
ans: A loan contract for a cargo shipment from Muziris to Alexandria
why: It documents the financing of a cargo of spices, ivory and textiles carried on the ship Hermapollon. It illustrates the scale of Indo-Roman trade.
extra: Muziris was located on the Kerala coast.

q: The holotype of Spinosaurus aegyptiacus, described by Ernst Stromer, was lost when:
opts: It was stolen from Cairo in 1952
Allied bombing destroyed the Munich museum in 1944
It was flooded in a Nile expedition
It was sold at auction in the 1920s
ans: Allied bombing destroyed the Munich museum in 1944
why: Stromer's original remains from Egypt, described in 1915, were destroyed during World War II. Only his published drawings and notes survived.
extra: New fossils from Morocco in the 2000s and 2010s renewed arguments about how aquatic Spinosaurus was.

q: Which Bronze Age town on Santorini, buried by the Minoan eruption, preserved well-known frescoes?
why: Volcanic ash buried the town in the 17th century BCE, preserving multi-storey buildings and wall paintings. No bodies were found, which suggests the inhabitants had left.
extra: The date of the eruption has been debated between radiocarbon and archaeological chronologies.

q: Isolated woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about:
why: Wrangel mammoths lived on after mainland populations were gone and were still alive when the Egyptian pyramids were being built. Genome studies show inbreeding and loss of genetic diversity.
extra: The island population was small and relatively dwarfed.

q: Anomalocaris, a large Cambrian predator, belongs to which group?
why: Radiodonts had large grasping frontal appendages and circular toothed mouths. Appendages alone were once mistaken for shrimp, and a mouth for a jellyfish.
extra: Whittington and Briggs published a major reconstruction in 1985.

q: Some scholars argue that Aboriginal Australian stories of drowned coastal lands may preserve memories of:
opts: Post-glacial sea-level rise over 7,000 years ago
ans: Post-glacial sea-level rise over 7,000 years ago
why: Sea levels rose by over 100 metres at the end of the last Ice Age, submerging large coastal areas. A 2016 study compared stories with reconstructed coastlines.
extra: The idea remains debated because oral tradition can change over time.

q: Rajasaurus narmadensis, a crested Late Cretaceous predator from India, belongs to which dinosaur group?
why: Rajasaurus was found in the Lameta Formation of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. Abelisaurids, with short deep skulls and tiny forelimbs, were dominant predators of the southern landmasses.
extra: Close relatives such as Majungasaurus from Madagascar reflect Gondwanan links between India and Madagascar.

q: Who analysed myths as structured by binary oppositions in works such as The Raw and the Cooked?
why: Levi-Strauss developed structural anthropology, proposing that myths share underlying mental structures. His work drew on linguistics.
extra: He studied Amazonian myths extensively.

q: Which element, enriched in the clay at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary, led the Alvarez team in 1980 to propose an asteroid impact?
why: Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but abundant in many asteroids, so a global spike at the boundary suggested extraterrestrial input. The Chicxulub crater in Yucatan was later identified as the impact site.
extra: The impact occurred about 66 million years ago.

q: In the Egyptian Book of the Dead, a heart that failed the weighing against the feather of Ma'at was devoured by:
why: The composite monster, part lion, hippopotamus and crocodile, waited beside the scales. Anubis supervised the weighing and Thoth recorded the verdict.
extra: The feather symbolised truth and cosmic order.

q: In which parva of the Mahabharata is the Bhagavad Gita found?
why: The Gita occurs just before the Kurukshetra war begins, when Krishna advises Arjuna on duty. It makes up chapters 23 to 40 of the Bhishma Parva.
extra: The Mahabharata has roughly 100,000 verses.

q: Which Chinese Lagerstätte, about 518 million years old, preserves early craniates such as Myllokunmingia?
why: The Chengjiang deposit preserves a wide range of Cambrian animals in great detail. Myllokunmingia is considered one of the earliest craniate or vertebrate-like animals.
extra: It is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Why do cephalopod eyes lack the blind spot found in vertebrate eyes?
opts: Their photoreceptors face the light, with nerve fibres behind the retina
They have two optic nerves per eye
Their retinas have no nerve fibres at all
They process vision only in the arms
ans: Their photoreceptors face the light, with nerve fibres behind the retina
why: In vertebrates the nerve fibres lie in front of the photoreceptors and exit through a gap, creating a blind spot. In cephalopods the retina is everted, so no gap is needed.
extra: Cephalopod and vertebrate camera eyes are a textbook case of convergent evolution.

q: Mesopotamian texts refer to the Indus region as:
why: Sumerian and Akkadian sources mention trade with Meluhha in carnelian and other goods. Indus-style seals and beads have been found at Mesopotamian sites.
extra: Dilmun is usually identified with Bahrain and Magan with Oman.

q: Roughly how much Neanderthal DNA do people outside Africa carry on average?
why: Interbreeding occurred after modern humans left Africa. Some inherited variants affect immunity, skin and hair.
extra: Sub-Saharan Africans carry small amounts via back-migration.

q: Hallucigenia, once reconstructed upside down, is now regarded as related to which living group?
why: Studies of its claws and spines, notably by Smith and Caron in 2015, placed Hallucigenia among lobopodians close to the ancestry of velvet worms. Early reconstructions mistook its spines for legs.
extra: Velvet worms are living relatives of arthropods and tardigrades within the Panarthropoda.

q: Ancient DNA from Rakhigarhi (2019) reported that the individual lacked ancestry from:
why: The study found a mix of Iranian-related and South Asian hunter-gatherer ancestry. It did not show Steppe-related ancestry, which appears in South Asia later.
extra: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is one of the largest Harappan sites.

q: Sinosauropteryx, announced in 1996, was significant as:
opts: The first non-avian dinosaur found with filamentous feather-like structures
The first dinosaur with true flight feathers
The first fossil proven to be warm-blooded
ans: The first non-avian dinosaur found with filamentous feather-like structures
why: The small theropod from Liaoning, China, had a covering of simple filaments called protofeathers. This finding strongly supported the dinosaur-bird link.
extra: Later analysis of its melanosomes suggested a banded tail.

q: Footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to about 21,000-23,000 years ago suggest:
opts: Humans were in the Americas long before the Clovis culture
ans: Humans were in the Americas long before the Clovis culture
why: The prints were dated using seeds and other methods. Clovis is dated to about 13,000 years ago.
extra: Prints include those of teenagers and children.

q: The Permian-Triassic extinction, about 252 million years ago, is linked to massive volcanism in which region?
why: Huge eruptions released greenhouse gases and toxic compounds, contributing to warming and ocean acidification and anoxia. An estimated 80 to 95 percent of marine species disappeared.
extra: It is often called the Great Dying.

q: A fossil site with exceptionally preserved soft tissues is called a:
why: Lagerstätten preserve soft anatomy, skin, feathers or organs, usually thanks to rapid burial in low-oxygen conditions. Examples include Burgess Shale, Solnhofen and Messel.
extra: The term comes from German for a 'storage place' or mine.

q: Excavations at Keezhadi in Tamil Nadu are significant because they have yielded:
opts: Potsherds inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi from a Sangam-era settlement
ans: Potsherds inscribed in Tamil-Brahmi from a Sangam-era settlement
why: The site shows an urban habitation in the Vaigai valley. The Tamil Nadu archaeology department has dated its early phases to around the 6th century BCE.
extra: The findings support the existence of early literacy in Tamil Nadu.

q: How long after its discovery in 1741 was Steller's sea cow hunted to extinction?
why: Georg Steller encountered the giant sirenian near the Commander Islands and the last was reportedly killed in 1768. Hunters had come for meat and fat during fur-trade voyages.
extra: It reached about 8 to 9 metres in length.

q: Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of which people?
why: The stone enclosures were built between the 11th and 15th centuries by Bantu-speaking people. Colonial writers falsely attributed it to outsiders.
extra: The name derives from words meaning 'stone houses'.

q: The 1848 injury of railway worker Phineas Gage, in which an iron rod passed through his skull, is most famous for implicating which brain region in personality and decision-making?
why: Gage survived with damage to his left frontal lobe, and contemporaries reported changes in his behaviour. Later accounts suggest the changes were exaggerated and that he partly recovered.
extra: He later worked as a stagecoach driver in Chile for years.

q: Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Australian Aboriginal language, are known for describing positions using what?
opts: Absolute cardinal directions rather than left and right
ans: Absolute cardinal directions rather than left and right
why: Stephen Levinson and John Haviland found speakers say things like 'the cup is to the north of the plate' and keep track of orientation constantly.
extra: This is cited as a case where language influences spatial cognition.

q: Roger Sperry's Nobel Prize-winning split-brain studies involved patients in whom which structure had been surgically cut?
why: Cutting the corpus callosum to control epilepsy left the two hemispheres unable to share information directly, revealing their specialisations.
extra: Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize with Hubel and Wiesel.

q: MacArthur and Wilson's theory of island biogeography predicts that species richness on an island depends on what?
opts: Island size and distance from the mainland
ans: Island size and distance from the mainland
why: Larger islands have lower extinction rates and nearer islands have higher colonisation rates, so the balance sets species number.
extra: The theory has been applied to nature reserve design.

q: Which volcano is the highest in the world above sea level, at about 6,893 m on the Chile-Argentina border?
why: Ojos del Salado in the Andes is the highest volcano on Earth and has fumarolic activity. Mauna Kea is taller from base to summit, but most of it is underwater.
extra: Mauna Kea stands about 4,207 m above sea level but over 10,000 m from the ocean floor.

q: Which anthropologist challenged Margaret Mead's portrayal of Samoan adolescence in Coming of Age in Samoa?
why: Freeman argued in 1983 that Mead had been misled by her informants and overstated Samoan sexual freedom. Many anthropologists regard his critique as overstated, and the debate continues.
extra: Mead's mentor was Franz Boas.

q: What does the Allee effect describe?
opts: Reduced individual fitness at low population density
ans: Reduced individual fitness at low population density
why: For example, small populations can struggle to find mates or defend against predators, so they may decline further.
extra: It is named after the ecologist Warder Clyde Allee.

q: Who created Esperanto, published in 1887?
why: Zamenhof, an ophthalmologist from Bialystok, designed Esperanto as an easy neutral international language.
extra: Schleyer created the earlier Volapuk.

q: Which principle, summarised as 'cells that fire together wire together', underlies many models of learning?
why: Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 that synapses strengthen when a presynaptic neuron repeatedly helps fire a postsynaptic one.
extra: The catchy slogan was later coined by the neuroscientist Carla Shatz.

q: The gharial, a critically endangered crocodilian of the Indian subcontinent, is notable for what feature?
opts: A long narrow snout specialised for catching fish
ans: A long narrow snout specialised for catching fish
why: Mature males have a bulbous growth on the snout tip called the ghara.
extra: The Chambal River holds one of its last strongholds.

q: In Simons and Chabris's 1999 'invisible gorilla' experiment, many viewers failed to notice a gorilla because of what?
why: People focused on counting basketball passes often missed an unexpected gorilla walking through the scene.
extra: About half of the participants failed to see it.

q: What makes the tigers of the Sundarbans mangroves unusual?
opts: They routinely swim and hunt in a tidal, brackish mangrove habitat
ans: They routinely swim and hunt in a tidal, brackish mangrove habitat
why: The Sundarbans tigers cross channels and take prey in saline conditions, which is uncommon among tigers.
extra: The Sundarbans, shared by India and Bangladesh, is the largest mangrove forest in the world.

q: Svante Paabo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for what?
opts: Identifying the first human language gene
Sequencing the Neanderthal genome and discovering the Denisovans
ans: Sequencing the Neanderthal genome and discovering the Denisovans
why: Paabo pioneered the extraction and sequencing of ancient DNA, producing the first Neanderthal genome and revealing Denisovans through DNA alone.
extra: His work also showed gene flow from Neanderthals into the ancestors of present-day non-Africans.

q: Which Kalidasa play, translated into English by Sir William Jones in 1789, was praised by Goethe?
why: The play tells of King Dushyanta and Shakuntala, whose recognition ring drives the plot. European readers first met Sanskrit drama through its translations.
extra: Mricchakatika is by Shudraka, Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta and Ratnavali by Harsha.

q: The first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star in 1995, which earned Mayor and Queloz a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize, was what kind of planet?
why: 51 Pegasi b is a gas giant with half of Jupiter's mass orbiting just 0.05 AU from its star in about 4.2 days. Such a planet was unexpected by planet-formation models.
extra: It was detected through the Doppler wobble of its star.

q: The epic of Sundiata, about the founder of the Mali Empire, has been preserved mainly by which West African tradition?
why: Griots memorise and perform genealogies and epics, passing them down through families.
extra: D. T. Niane published a well-known written version based on a griot's telling.

q: The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with which body of water?
why: The strait lies between Iran and Oman's Musandam peninsula and opens into the Gulf of Oman and then the Arabian Sea. It is one of the world's most important oil chokepoints.
extra: Roughly a fifth of global petroleum consumption passes through it.

q: Which Tamil classic, attributed to Thiruvalluvar, consists of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love?
why: The Thirukkural is arranged in 133 chapters of ten couplets each, and is one of the most translated works in Tamil.
extra: A 133-foot statue of Thiruvalluvar stands at Kanyakumari.

q: What chiefly keeps the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica free of ice and snow?
opts: A layer of dark volcanic dust
Katabatic winds that sublimate snow and ice
ans: Katabatic winds that sublimate snow and ice
why: Cold, dense air pouring down from the polar plateau warms as it descends and is extremely dry, so it removes snow and ice by sublimation. The surrounding mountains also block glaciers from flowing in.
extra: NASA uses the valleys as an analogue environment for Mars.

q: How far back does the EPICA Dome C Antarctic ice core record, the longest continuous ice-core climate record so far?
why: Air bubbles trapped in the ice preserve ancient atmospheres, showing carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together across eight glacial cycles.
extra: Carbon dioxide in that record never exceeded roughly 300 parts per million before the industrial era.

q: What gives the caustic, alkaline Lake Natron in Tanzania its red and orange hues?
why: Haloarchaea and cyanobacteria thrive in the lake's extreme salinity and alkalinity and tint the water, especially when evaporation concentrates the brine. Flamingos breed there because few predators can reach the nests.
extra: The lake's water gets its sodium carbonate chemistry from nearby Ol Doinyo Lengai, the only volcano to erupt natrocarbonatite lava.

q: Cassini discovered plumes of water vapour and ice erupting from the south pole of which Saturnian moon?
why: The plumes sample a subsurface ocean and contain salts, silica and organic molecules, hinting at hydrothermal activity.
extra: The plumes supply material to Saturn's E ring.

q: Which hunter-gatherer people of Tanzania, living near Lake Eyasi and speaking a click language, are widely studied as a window into foraging lifeways?
why: The Hadza forage for tubers, honey and game and live in flexible camps. Their way of life has been used to study cooperation, mobility and sleep patterns in small-scale societies.
extra: Their language is considered an isolate, unrelated to other known languages.

q: Under the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which country holds sovereignty over Svalbard while citizens of the signatory states may live and work there freely?
why: The treaty recognises Norwegian sovereignty but gives nationals of signatory states equal rights to residence and economic activity. Norwegian law applies, with limits on militarisation.
extra: Russia still operates the coal-mining settlement of Barentsburg on Svalbard.

q: Roughly what fraction of an octopus's neurons are located in its arms?
why: An octopus has around 500 million neurons, with most in the arms, which can control their movement semi-independently of the brain.
extra: Octopus lineages diverged from ours more than 500 million years ago, so its intelligence evolved independently.

q: What did the S-wave shadow zone reveal about Earth's interior?
opts: The crust is detached from the mantle
why: S-waves are shear waves and cannot travel through liquids. Their failure to arrive on the far side of Earth showed that the outer core is liquid.
extra: P-waves, which can pass through liquids, are refracted at the core and form their own shadow zone.

q: Which country has the highest lowest point of any country, at roughly 1,400 m above sea level?
why: Lesotho's lowest point lies where the Makhaleng River meets the Orange River at about 1,400 m. The whole country is above 1,000 m, earning it the nickname 'Kingdom in the Sky'.
extra: It is entirely surrounded by South Africa.

q: Algal blooms fed by fertiliser runoff create ocean 'dead zones' mainly by causing what?
opts: Oxygen depletion as the algae decompose
ans: Oxygen depletion as the algae decompose
why: Bacteria decomposing dead algae use up oxygen, leaving water too low in oxygen for most animals.
extra: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is fed by Mississippi River nutrients.

q: Which moon, visited by the Huygens probe in 2005, has stable lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane?
why: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and its surface temperature of about minus 180 degrees allows methane to rain and pool.
extra: NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is planned to explore Titan, with launch expected in 2028.

q: What is the main resolution of Olbers' paradox, which asks why the night sky is dark?
opts: Interstellar dust absorbs all distant starlight
Space is opaque beyond a certain distance
The Universe has a finite age, so light from very distant stars has not all reached us
Stars are too sparse to fill the sky
ans: The Universe has a finite age, so light from very distant stars has not all reached us
why: If the Universe were infinite, eternal and static, every line of sight would end on a star. Finite age and cosmic expansion remove that conclusion. Dust would heat up and glow, so it does not solve the problem.
extra: Edgar Allan Poe proposed the finite-age solution in his 1848 prose poem Eureka.

q: Manitoulin Island, the largest island in any freshwater lake, lies in which lake?
why: Manitoulin Island, in Ontario, sits in Lake Huron and is the largest lake island in the world. It is itself large enough to contain many lakes.
extra: Its Lake Manitou is the largest lake on a lake island, and it has islands of its own.

q: At roughly what rate is the Himalayan range currently being uplifted?
why: The Himalayas are still rising because India continues to push into Eurasia, causing thrust faulting and crustal thickening. Uplift is a few millimetres a year, while erosion removes some of the gain.
extra: India is converging with Eurasia at roughly 4 to 5 cm per year, most of which is absorbed by crustal shortening.

q: Which change, roughly between 1400 and 1700, altered English long vowels and helps explain irregular spelling?
why: Long vowels shifted upwards in the mouth, so that 'bite', once pronounced like 'beet', changed. Spelling had by then largely been fixed.
extra: The causes of the shift remain debated.

q: In English, aspirated [p-h] in 'pin' and unaspirated [p] in 'spin' are examples of what?
why: Allophones are variants of a phoneme that don't change word meaning in the language. English speakers ignore the aspiration difference.
extra: In Hindi, aspiration is phonemic: pal and phal are different words.

q: Around 5.3 million years ago, the Zanclean flood refilled which basin after it had largely dried out?
why: During the Messinian Salinity Crisis the Mediterranean's link to the Atlantic closed and the basin evaporated, leaving thick salt deposits. An abrupt breach near Gibraltar then refilled it.
extra: Evaporite deposits up to a couple of kilometres thick still lie beneath the Mediterranean seafloor.

q: The sentence 'The horse raced past the barn fell' is a classic example of what?
why: Readers first parse 'raced' as the main verb, then must reanalyse it as a reduced relative clause.
extra: Such sentences are used to study how people process syntax incrementally.

q: Who became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913?
why: Tagore was honoured for the poems in Gitanjali, which he translated into English himself with W. B. Yeats writing the introduction. Kipling, born in Bombay, was British and won in 1907.
extra: Tagore wrote the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

q: V. S. Ramachandran's mirror box therapy aims to reduce phantom limb pain by doing what?
opts: Removing the remaining part of the limb
Giving visual feedback that the missing limb is moving
Blocking the sensory cortex with drugs
ans: Giving visual feedback that the missing limb is moving
why: A mirror reflects the intact limb so it appears that the missing limb is moving, which may resolve conflict between motor intention and visual feedback.
extra: Clinical trials show it helps some patients but not others.

q: Floating mats of vegetation called phumdis, which carry a national park, are found in which Indian lake?
why: Loktak Lake in Manipur has phumdis, floating masses of soil, vegetation and organic matter. Keibul Lamjao National Park, the world's only floating national park, sits on them.
extra: The park protects the sangai, the endangered brow-antlered deer.

q: Which Saadat Hasan Manto story is about inmates of a lunatic asylum being exchanged between India and Pakistan after Partition?
why: Bishan Singh, an inmate, refuses to leave his hometown and dies in the no-man's-land between the borders.
extra: The other titles are also Manto stories, but are not about the asylum.

q: Why do seismologists prefer moment magnitude (Mw) to the Richter scale for very large earthquakes?
opts: Mw is determined from the amount of building damage
The Richter scale saturates for large events, whereas Mw reflects fault area, slip and rock rigidity
Mw can be calculated without any seismometers
The Richter scale was designed only for volcanic tremors
ans: The Richter scale saturates for large events, whereas Mw reflects fault area, slip and rock rigidity
why: Richter-type scales underestimate the biggest quakes because the recorded wave amplitudes stop growing at high magnitude. Moment magnitude is based on the physical seismic moment, so it keeps scaling properly.
extra: The 1960 Valdivia, Chile, earthquake at Mw 9.5 is the largest ever recorded.

q: Which is the world's southernmost national capital?
why: Wellington, at about 41 degrees south, lies farther south than the capitals of Australia, Argentina or Chile. It is also known for strong winds funnelled through Cook Strait.
extra: The city is crossed by the active Wellington Fault, which makes it highly exposed to earthquakes.

q: Which Milankovitch cycle operates on a period of roughly 100,000 years?
why: Eccentricity describes how elliptical Earth's orbit is, varying on cycles of about 100,000 and 400,000 years. Tilt varies over about 41,000 years and precession over roughly 19,000 to 26,000 years.
extra: Oddly, the 100,000-year cycle dominates ice-age rhythms of the past million years even though its direct forcing is weakest.

q: Which literary movement in Hindi poetry, c. 1918 to 1938, was romantic and mystical, with poets such as Prasad, Pant, Nirala and Mahadevi Verma?
why: Chhayavad poets used nature, symbolism and subjective emotion. Prasad's Kamayani is a major work of the movement.
extra: The four poets are known as its 'chaar stambh', or four pillars.

q: Why does energy-producing fusion in massive stars stop at iron?
opts: Fusing iron absorbs energy instead of releasing it
Iron nuclei are too large to collide
The star runs out of iron
Iron is too radioactive to fuse
ans: Fusing iron absorbs energy instead of releasing it
why: Iron-group nuclei have the highest binding energy per nucleon, so further fusion consumes energy. The core then loses support and collapses.
extra: The collapse triggers a core-collapse supernova.

q: Networks of which organisms link plant roots and can move carbon and nutrients between trees, sometimes called the 'wood wide web'?
why: Mycorrhizal fungi form symbiotic associations with roots and connect plants underground.
extra: The extent to which trees benefit each other through these networks is debated.

q: Roughly what fraction of the body's energy at rest does the human brain consume?
why: The brain is about 2% of body mass but uses around a fifth of the resting energy supply, mainly to restore ion gradients after neural signalling.
extra: The brain depends heavily on glucose and oxygen.

q: Which object, detected in 2017, was the first confirmed interstellar visitor to the Solar System?
why: 'Oumuamua followed a hyperbolic path that proved it came from outside the Solar System, and it was oddly elongated and accelerated non-gravitationally.
extra: 2I/Borisov was the second, and 3I/ATLAS, found in 2025, the third.

q: The Bijak is a major compilation of verses attributed to which Bhakti poet-saint?
why: The Bijak was compiled by followers of the Kabir Panth. Kabir criticised ritualism in both Hinduism and Islam.
extra: Some of his verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib.

q: The Piraha language, studied by Daniel Everett for claims about recursion and number words, is spoken in which country?
why: Piraha is spoken by a small community on the Maici River in the Brazilian Amazon. Everett argued it lacks recursion and exact number words, a claim that is controversial.
extra: It has one of the smallest phoneme inventories known.

q: The Indian Ocean Dipole refers to differences in what?
opts: Tidal range on the two sides of the ocean
Monsoon onset dates between India and East Africa
Sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean
Salinity between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal
ans: Sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean
why: A positive dipole has a warmer western and cooler eastern Indian Ocean, shifting rainfall towards East Africa and away from Indonesia and Australia.
extra: A positive dipole can offset the monsoon-weakening effect of El Nino, as seen in some years.

q: In which animal were mirror neurons first reported in the 1990s?
why: Giacomo Rizzolatti's group in Parma recorded premotor neurons that fired both when a monkey performed a grasping action and when it watched one.
extra: Their role in human empathy and language remains debated.

q: What veterinary drug caused the collapse of South Asia's vulture populations in the 1990s?
why: Vultures eating carcasses of cattle treated with diclofenac suffered kidney failure.
extra: India banned veterinary use of diclofenac in 2006, and populations have stabilised.

q: Which novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (1882) contains the song 'Vande Mataram'?
why: The novel is set during the Sannyasi rebellion of the 18th century in Bengal.
extra: Tagore sang the song at the 1896 session of the Indian National Congress.

q: Unlike most large peninsular Indian rivers, the Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea. What geological feature does it follow?
why: The Narmada and the Tapi occupy rift (graben) valleys between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges. This is why they flow westward and form estuaries rather than deltas.
extra: Most peninsular rivers, such as the Godavari and Krishna, flow east towards the Bay of Bengal.

q: Which country has the most languages of any nation, with around 840?
why: Papua New Guinea's rugged terrain and small communities led to extreme linguistic diversity.
extra: Tok Pisin, an English-based creole, serves as a common language.

q: Which of these countries is doubly landlocked, meaning every one of its neighbours is itself landlocked?
why: All five of Uzbekistan's neighbours (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan) lack an ocean coast, so no single border crossing leads to the sea. Kazakhstan borders Russia and China, which do have coasts.
extra: The only other doubly landlocked country is Liechtenstein.

q: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Italian for what duration?
why: Venice and Ragusa required ships to wait forty days, quaranta giorni, during plague outbreaks.
extra: The number forty may have echoed biblical forty-day periods.

q: The East African Rift is slowly splitting Africa into which two plates?
why: Rifting along the East African Rift system is separating the larger Nubian plate from the smaller Somali plate. In time it could open a new ocean basin.
extra: A large crack that appeared in Kenya in 2018 after heavy rain was due to erosion of volcanic ash, not plate splitting.

q: The English word 'muscle' derives from a Latin word meaning what?
why: Latin musculus is a diminutive of mus, mouse, probably because a flexing muscle looks like a mouse moving under the skin.
extra: Anatomical terms often come from Latin and Greek metaphors.

q: Roughly what percentage of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next, on average?
why: Most energy is lost as heat in metabolism, so food chains rarely exceed four or five levels.
extra: The figure varies and can range from a few to about 20 percent.

q: Who was the first recipient of the Jnanpith Award, in 1965?
why: The Malayalam poet was honoured for his collection Odakkuzhal.
extra: Tarashankar Bandyopadhyay won the next year.

q: In volcanology, what is a lahar?
opts: A volcanic mudflow of water, ash and debris
A cloud of sulfur dioxide gas
A glowing avalanche of hot gas and rock
A tunnel through which lava flows
ans: A volcanic mudflow of water, ash and debris
why: Lahars form when volcanic debris mixes with water from melting ice, rain or crater lakes and races down valleys with the consistency of wet concrete.
extra: Lahars from Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia buried the town of Armero in 1985, killing around 23,000 people.

q: What does the acronym WEIRD, introduced by Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan in 2010, describe?
opts: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic study populations
ans: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic study populations
why: The authors pointed out that most psychology and behavioural experiments use participants from a thin slice of humanity, which may make results unrepresentative.
extra: Cross-cultural studies show that things like fairness norms and perceptual illusions vary across societies.

q: From where do poison dart frogs obtain the alkaloids that make them toxic?
opts: Their diet of ants, mites and other arthropods
ans: Their diet of ants, mites and other arthropods
why: Frogs sequester the chemicals from prey, which is why captive frogs fed fruit flies are not toxic.
extra: Their bright colours warn predators.

q: Which celestial feature have some dung beetles been shown to use to keep rolling dung balls in straight lines at night?
why: Experiments in a planetarium showed that beetles orient using the band of light from the Milky Way on moonless nights.
extra: This was reported in 2013 by Marie Dacke and colleagues.

q: In the International Phonetic Alphabet, the first sound of English 'think' is described as what?
why: The sound is made with the tongue against the teeth and air flowing through a gap without vocal cord vibration.
extra: Many languages lack it, and learners often substitute dental stops.

q: Observations of which type of exploding star revealed in 1998 that the Universe's expansion is accelerating?
why: Type Ia supernovae have nearly uniform peak brightness, so they work as standard candles. Distant ones appeared fainter than expected, indicating accelerating expansion.
extra: The discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess.

q: Devanagari is classified as which type of writing system?
why: In an abugida, each consonant carries an inherent vowel that is modified by diacritics. Devanagari uses this principle.
extra: The term comes from the Ge'ez script of Ethiopia.

q: True or false: a high-altitude adaptation variant of the EPAS1 gene found in many Tibetans was inherited from Denisovans.
why: The Tibetan variant reduces the overproduction of red blood cells at low oxygen and matches a Denisovan haplotype. It appears to have entered the ancestors of Tibetans through interbreeding and then spread under natural selection.
extra: A Denisovan jaw from Baishiya Karst Cave in Tibet, at about 3,280 m, shows that Denisovans lived at high altitude.

q: Lonar Lake in Maharashtra, a saline soda lake, was formed by what?
opts: The cutoff of a river meander
why: The lake occupies an impact crater about 1.8 km across, formed in Deccan basalt tens to hundreds of thousands of years ago. It is one of very few known impact craters in basaltic rock.
extra: Planetary scientists study it as an analogue for impact craters on the Moon and Mars.

q: Why do tropical cyclones almost never form within about 5 degrees of the Equator?
opts: The sea surface is too cold
The Coriolis effect is too weak to start rotation
Wind shear there is always too strong
ans: The Coriolis effect is too weak to start rotation
why: Cyclones need the Coriolis force to deflect inflowing air into a spiral. Near the Equator that force is nearly zero, so organised rotation does not develop.
extra: Typhoon Vamei in December 2001 formed at about 1.5 degrees north, a very rare exception.

q: Which parasite reduces rodents' innate fear of cat odour, apparently helping it return to its definitive host?
why: Infected rodents lose aversion to the scent of cats, increasing the chance of predation and thus of the parasite reaching a cat.
extra: Roughly a quarter to a third of humans carry the parasite.

q: Which of these Antarctic features is among the saltiest bodies of water on Earth, staying liquid at around -50 degrees Celsius?
why: Don Juan Pond is saturated with calcium chloride, which depresses its freezing point so much that it almost never freezes. Its salinity is higher than that of the Dead Sea.
extra: NASA studies it as an analogue for possible liquid brines on Mars.

q: What does memory reconsolidation research suggest happens when a stored memory is recalled?
opts: It becomes temporarily unstable and can be modified before being stored again
It moves to a different brain region
ans: It becomes temporarily unstable and can be modified before being stored again
why: Karim Nader's 2000 experiments showed that blocking protein synthesis after recall can weaken a consolidated memory.
extra: This is being explored for treatments of traumatic memories.

q: Brahui, a Dravidian language, is spoken mainly in which country?
why: Brahui is spoken in Balochistan, far from the Dravidian heartland in South India, surrounded by Indo-Iranian languages.
extra: Some scholars see it as a relic of an older Dravidian presence in northwest South Asia, but this is debated.

q: Robin Dunbar proposed that humans can maintain about how many stable social relationships?
why: Dunbar linked primate group size to neocortex size and extrapolated to humans, predicting group sizes near 150. Village and band sizes in many societies cluster around that figure.
extra: The number is debated, and its use for online networks is contested.

q: Which Russian author was sentenced to death in 1849 and reprieved at the last moment before a firing squad?
why: He was arrested with the Petrashevsky Circle and, after the mock execution, sent to a Siberian labour camp for four years.
extra: The experience informed novels such as The Idiot.

q: The first rogue wave measured by an instrument, in 1995, struck which North Sea platform?
why: A laser sensor on the Draupner platform recorded a wave about 25.6 m high on 1 January 1995, far larger than the surrounding sea state. It showed that rogue waves are real and not just sailors' tales.
extra: Rogue waves are generally defined as at least twice the significant wave height of the surrounding seas.

q: Patient H.M. (Henry Molaison), who lost his hippocampi in 1953 surgery, could still learn which kind of memory?
opts: Procedural memory, such as mirror-drawing skills
ans: Procedural memory, such as mirror-drawing skills
why: H.M. could not form new conscious memories of events but improved on motor tasks without remembering practising them. This showed that memory systems are separable.
extra: Brenda Milner's studies of him founded modern memory neuroscience.

q: Why does the sickle-cell allele remain common in regions with endemic malaria?
opts: It increases the lifespan of people with two copies
Carriers with one copy have greater resistance to severe malaria
It makes red blood cells divide faster
ans: Carriers with one copy have greater resistance to severe malaria
why: Carriers with one copy of the allele are protected against severe malaria, while two copies cause sickle-cell disease. This balancing selection keeps the allele frequency high.
extra: The allele is also frequent in several tribal populations of central and western India.

q: Which Punjabi poet wrote the Partition lament addressed to Waris Shah, 'Ajj Aakhaan Waris Shah Nu'?
why: The poem calls on the 18th-century poet of Heer to witness the horrors of 1947.
extra: Pritam won the Jnanpith Award in 1981.

q: True or false: in human evolution, large brains evolved before upright bipedal walking.
why: Bipedalism appeared millions of years before the brain expanded. Early hominins like Australopithecus afarensis walked upright with ape-sized brains.
extra: Brain expansion accelerated with Homo, beginning roughly two million years ago.

q: Which eruption caused the 1816 'Year Without a Summer'?
why: The April 1815 eruption of Tambora in Indonesia injected huge amounts of sulfate aerosols into the stratosphere. These reflected sunlight and cooled the climate, causing crop failures in the Northern Hemisphere.
extra: The gloomy summer of 1816 is linked to the writing of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein in Geneva.

q: Why do space agencies steer large decommissioned spacecraft towards a patch of the South Pacific known as Point Nemo?
opts: It has the calmest weather on Earth
It has the strongest magnetic field
It lies directly beneath the International Date Line
It is the point farthest from any land
ans: It is the point farthest from any land
why: Point Nemo, an oceanic pole of inaccessibility, lies roughly 2,700 km from the nearest land, so debris surviving re-entry is very unlikely to endanger anyone. Dozens of spacecraft have been disposed of there.
extra: It is named after Captain Nemo from Jules Verne's novels, and the ISS is expected to be deorbited there.

q: The supermassive black hole Sagittarius A* at the centre of the Milky Way has a mass of about how many Suns?
why: Its mass was determined from the orbits of stars such as S2 around it, work that earned Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize.
extra: The star S2 orbits it in about 16 years.

q: Which two countries border the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad Oblast?
why: Kaliningrad, formerly Konigsberg, is cut off from the rest of Russia by Lithuania and Poland. It gives Russia an ice-free Baltic port.
extra: The philosopher Immanuel Kant was born, lived and is buried in Konigsberg.

q: Which moon is the most volcanically active body in the solar system?
why: Io's interior is flexed by tidal forces from Jupiter and the orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede, producing intense heating and hundreds of volcanoes.
extra: Its volcanic plumes can rise hundreds of kilometres.

q: Roughly how fast is the Atlantic Ocean widening at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
why: New crust forms at the ridge and the plates move apart at a few centimetres a year. This is about the rate at which fingernails grow.
extra: Spreading is much faster at the East Pacific Rise, where rates exceed 10 cm per year.

q: Loss of which neuropeptide-producing neurons in the hypothalamus causes narcolepsy type 1?
why: Orexin neurons promote wakefulness and stabilise sleep-wake transitions. Their loss leads to sudden sleep attacks and cataplexy.
extra: Drugs that block orexin receptors are used as insomnia treatments.

q: Whose travel journal Oku no Hosomichi (Narrow Road to the Deep North) is a landmark of Japanese haibun?
why: In this 17th-century work, Basho blends prose and haiku to record a journey through northern Japan.
extra: He elevated haikai into a serious art form.

q: Which writing system was deliberately designed in the 15th century by a king and court scholars, with consonant shapes modelled on speech organs?
why: King Sejong the Great had Hangul created in 1443 and promulgated in 1446 to make writing accessible. Its letters reflect articulatory features.
extra: Hangul Day in Korea is celebrated on 9 October.

q: True or false: Antarctica is classified as a desert, and it is the largest desert on Earth.
why: Deserts are defined by low precipitation, not by heat, and most of Antarctica receives very little. Parts of its interior get only a few tens of millimetres of water-equivalent a year.
extra: The Sahara is the largest hot desert, but the Antarctic and Arctic polar deserts are larger.

q: A fossil called Denisova 11, found in 2018, was a girl with what parentage?
opts: A Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
A Homo erectus mother and a Denisovan father
A Homo sapiens mother and a Neanderthal father
ans: A Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father
why: Genome analysis showed the girl's mother was Neanderthal and her father Denisovan. It was the first direct evidence of a first-generation hybrid between two archaic human groups.
extra: Her father also carried Neanderthal ancestry from earlier interbreeding.

q: Which glutamate receptor acts as a coincidence detector central to long-term potentiation?
why: The NMDA receptor opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is depolarised, which relieves a magnesium block and lets calcium in.
extra: Ketamine and memantine act on NMDA receptors.

q: In which language did Rumi compose his Masnavi?
why: Rumi wrote the Masnavi in Konya, in Anatolia, in the 13th century.
extra: The Masnavi is often called the Quran in Persian by admirers.

q: Which is the largest moon in the solar system and the only one known to generate its own magnetic field?
why: Ganymede, larger than Mercury, has an intrinsic magnetic field detected by the Galileo spacecraft in the 1990s. It also probably has a subsurface ocean.
extra: ESA's JUICE mission, launched in 2023, is due to orbit Ganymede in the 2030s.

q: In which of these languages are click consonants part of the sound system?
why: Xhosa and Zulu use clicks, borrowed from contact with Khoe-San languages. Swahili, Amharic and Hausa have none.
extra: The letter x in Xhosa stands for a lateral click.

q: What is blindsight?
opts: Responding to objects in a blind visual field without conscious awareness
Seeing without eyes using other senses
Enhanced night vision after eye damage
ans: Responding to objects in a blind visual field without conscious awareness
why: Some people with damage to the primary visual cortex can point at or avoid objects in the blind region while insisting they see nothing.
extra: It likely relies on alternative pathways, such as through the superior colliculus.

q: Where is most of the body's serotonin produced?
opts: In the raphe nuclei of the brain
why: About 90% of the body's serotonin is made by enterochromaffin cells in the gut lining.
extra: Gut serotonin does not cross the blood-brain barrier, and the brain makes its own.

q: North Sentinel Island, home to the isolated Sentinelese people, is part of which Indian Union Territory?
why: Indian law bans approaching the island closely and protects the Sentinelese from outside contact. Their low immunity to common diseases is a major reason for the policy.
extra: The island lies in the Bay of Bengal, west of the Andaman Islands.

q: Which river is the longest in Europe?
why: The Volga, about 3,500 km long, rises northwest of Moscow and flows entirely within Russia. The Danube, Europe's second-longest river, is shorter.
extra: The Volga drains into the Caspian Sea, so it never reaches an ocean.

q: What does Chomsky's sentence 'Colourless green ideas sleep furiously' illustrate?
opts: A sentence can be grammatical but meaningless
A sentence can be meaningful but ungrammatical
ans: A sentence can be grammatical but meaningless
why: The sentence follows English syntax but is semantically odd, showing that syntax and meaning are separable.
extra: It appeared in Chomsky's 1957 Syntactic Structures.

q: True or false: Africa is the only continent crossed by both the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
why: Both lines cross Africa, which therefore has land in all four hemispheres. No other continent is crossed by both.
extra: The intersection of the two lines lies in the Gulf of Guinea, at a spot informally called Null Island.

q: Genetic and linguistic evidence trace the ancestors of Polynesians to which region?
opts: Island Southeast Asia and Taiwan, through the Austronesian expansion
ans: Island Southeast Asia and Taiwan, through the Austronesian expansion
why: Polynesian languages belong to the Austronesian family, which originated in Taiwan. Lapita voyagers spread into the Pacific around 3,000 years ago.
extra: Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki idea of a South American origin was rejected, though genomes show limited Native American contact around 1200 CE.

q: Evidence of controlled fire from about one million years ago has been reported from which South African cave?
why: Microscopic ash and burnt bone at Wonderwerk were attributed to Homo erectus in 2012. It is among the earliest evidence for fire use that is widely discussed.
extra: Habitual fire use is more securely documented from around 400,000 years ago.

q: What is thought to have caused the 'Great Dimming' of Betelgeuse in 2019 to 2020?
opts: A dust cloud formed from material ejected from its cooled surface
A black hole drifting in front of it
The star beginning to collapse into a black hole
ans: A dust cloud formed from material ejected from its cooled surface
why: Observations indicate that a surface cooling event let ejected gas condense into dust, partly blocking the star's light.
extra: Betelgeuse will eventually explode as a supernova, but probably not within about 100,000 years.

q: Milman Parry and Albert Lord's study of Yugoslav oral poets led to what theory about the Homeric epics?
opts: That they were written by one literate poet in Athens
That they were copied from Egyptian sources
That they were composed orally using formulaic phrases and themes
ans: That they were composed orally using formulaic phrases and themes
why: Singers composed in performance using stock phrases that fit the metre, such as fixed epithets.
extra: The theory is called oral-formulaic composition.

q: Which early 11th-century work by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, is often regarded as one of the world's earliest novels?
why: The story follows Hikaru Genji, a prince, and his descendants. It runs to 54 chapters.
extra: The Pillow Book was written by her contemporary Sei Shonagon.

q: India lies within how many of the world's recognised biodiversity hotspots?
why: India includes the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands) hotspots.
extra: A hotspot has at least 1,500 endemic plant species and has lost at least 70% of its original habitat.

q: What produced the first gravitational waves ever detected directly, by LIGO in 2015?
opts: The merger of two black holes
A supernova in the Milky Way
ans: The merger of two black holes
why: The signal GW150914 came from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.
extra: A neutron star merger observed in 2017 was seen in both gravitational waves and light.

q: Which Shakespeare play includes the stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'?
why: Antigonus is killed by a bear on the coast of Bohemia, which has no real seacoast.
extra: The setting comes from Robert Greene's Pandosto, Shakespeare's source.

q: The Durand Line, drawn in 1893, forms the contested boundary between which two countries today?
why: The line was agreed between Sir Mortimer Durand of British India and the Afghan Amir Abdur Rahman Khan, and it split Pashtun lands. It is now the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
extra: Successive Afghan governments have disputed it as an international boundary.

q: In Benjamin Libet's 1980s experiments, what preceded people's reported conscious urge to move a finger?
opts: A build-up of brain activity called the readiness potential
A reflex arc in the spinal cord
ans: A build-up of brain activity called the readiness potential
why: The readiness potential began hundreds of milliseconds before awareness of intention, leading to arguments about free will.
extra: Later work suggests the signal may reflect random fluctuations rather than a decision.

q: The title of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart is drawn from a poem by which poet?
why: The poem is Yeats's 'The Second Coming', whose opening lines describe the breakdown of order.
extra: The novel was published in 1958.

q: Geetanjali Shree's Tomb of Sand, translated by Daisy Rockwell, was the first book translated from which language to win the International Booker Prize?
why: Ret Samadhi won in 2022, following novels written in English by authors of Indian origin that had won the main Booker Prize.
extra: Banu Mushtaq's Heart Lamp, a Kannada story collection translated by Deepa Bhasthi, won in 2025.

q: Which language family has the most languages, with about 1,500?
why: Niger-Congo languages include Swahili, Yoruba and Zulu. Indo-European has far more speakers but only about 450 languages.
extra: Austronesian is second in number of languages, with about 1,200.

q: Which pair of countries share the world's longest international land border?
why: The Canada-US boundary runs for about 8,900 km when the Alaska border is included. No other pair of countries shares a longer land frontier.
extra: Russia and Kazakhstan come second, at roughly 7,600 km.

q: Which country has the most islands in the world?
why: By counts of islands, islets and skerries, Sweden's coastal archipelagos, especially around Stockholm, give it roughly 267,000, far more than Indonesia's roughly 17,000. Only a small fraction of Sweden's islands are inhabited.
extra: Norway and Finland also have very high counts because glaciation carved their coasts into countless islets.

q: Why does the Antarctic ozone hole form over Antarctica rather than elsewhere?
opts: Antarctica is closest to the Sun in winter
Polar stratospheric clouds in the cold polar vortex enable chlorine to destroy ozone
There is no ozone there to begin with
ans: Polar stratospheric clouds in the cold polar vortex enable chlorine to destroy ozone
why: In the extreme winter cold, clouds provide surfaces on which reactions convert inert chlorine compounds into active forms. When sunlight returns in spring, these destroy ozone rapidly.
extra: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 phased out CFCs, and Antarctic ozone is expected to recover around the 2060s.

q: Which verse form did Milton use for Paradise Lost?
why: Milton rejected rhyme as a later barbarism and wanted to follow classical epic models.
extra: He dictated the poem after he had become blind.

q: Which Indian state shares international borders with both Bangladesh and Myanmar?
why: Mizoram borders Bangladesh to the west and Myanmar to the east and south. Tripura and Meghalaya touch only Bangladesh, and Manipur touches only Myanmar.
extra: Mizoram is among India's most heavily forested states.

q: Which British judge in Calcutta proposed in 1786 that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin share a common ancestral source?
why: Jones noted the structural and root similarities among Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, and other languages and suggested they had a shared origin. He founded the Asiatic Society in 1784.
extra: His observation launched comparative linguistics and the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European.

q: Which country spans the most time zones when its overseas territories are included?
why: France's overseas departments and territories, from French Guiana to French Polynesia, give it more time zones than any other country. Russia has the most on a single contiguous landmass.
extra: France is usually credited with 12 time zones, or 13 if its Antarctic claim is counted.

q: Which Indian state has the longest mainland coastline?
why: Gujarat's coastline of well over 1,000 km includes the Kutch and Kathiawar peninsulas and the Gulf of Khambhat. It is longer than that of any other mainland state.
extra: Among all states and union territories, only the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have more coastline.

q: Which major river crosses the Equator twice?
why: The Congo's basin straddles the Equator, so the river crosses it near Mbandaka and again further upstream. Because part of the basin is always in a rainy season, its discharge is unusually steady.
extra: The Congo is also the deepest known river in the world, with measured depths beyond 220 m.

q: Which brain region contains the majority of the brain's neurons?
why: The cerebellum holds roughly 80% of the brain's neurons, about 69 billion of 86 billion, despite being a small part of its volume.
extra: It is involved in movement coordination and also in cognition.

q: The Aral Sea shrank dramatically because water from which two rivers was diverted for irrigation?
why: Soviet irrigation schemes, mainly for cotton, took most of the inflow from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya from the 1960s on. The lake lost most of its area and left the Aralkum desert on its former bed.
extra: Dust storms from the exposed seabed carry salts and agricultural chemicals across the region.

q: Which community of northeast India follows a matrilineal system in which the youngest daughter inherits the ancestral property?
why: Among the Khasi of Meghalaya, descent is traced through the mother and the youngest daughter, the khatduh, takes care of the parents and inherits the clan property.
extra: The neighbouring Garo are also matrilineal, but political authority usually still rests with men.

q: What does the Wilson cycle describe?
opts: The repeated opening and closing of ocean basins through plate tectonics
The alternation of glacial and interglacial periods
The cycling of carbon between rocks and atmosphere
ans: The repeated opening and closing of ocean basins through plate tectonics
why: J. Tuzo Wilson proposed in the 1960s that ocean basins open by rifting, widen by spreading, and eventually close by subduction and collision. The cycle then restarts.
extra: The Atlantic is thought to have opened where the older Iapetus Ocean had closed.

q: Indira Point, the southernmost point of India, lies on which island?
why: Indira Point is at the southern tip of Great Nicobar, only about 150 km from Sumatra. The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake lowered land there by several metres.
extra: The 2004 tsunami damaged the Indira Point lighthouse and several nearby settlements.

q: What killed Otzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps in 1991?
opts: An arrowhead wound to the shoulder
ans: An arrowhead wound to the shoulder
why: CT scans in 2001 revealed an arrowhead lodged near his left subclavian artery, which would have caused fatal bleeding. A skull injury may also have contributed.
extra: His genome also revealed the oldest known case of the Lyme disease bacterium.

q: Placebo pain relief can be partly reversed by which opioid-blocking drug?
why: Because naloxone blocks opioid receptors and reduces placebo analgesia, the placebo effect must partly involve the body's own opioids.
extra: This shows that expectations can trigger real biochemical changes.

q: Coral bleaching occurs when corals expel which symbiotic organisms?
why: Heat stress makes the symbiotic algae leave the coral tissue, causing it to turn white.
extra: A fourth global bleaching event began in 2023.

q: How many countries does the Danube flow through?
why: The Danube passes through Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine, more than any other river in the world.
extra: It flows through four national capitals: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

q: Who composed the Ashtadhyayi, a Sanskrit grammar of about 4,000 concise rules?
why: Panini, working around the fourth century BCE, produced a precise rule system for Sanskrit that resembles a formal generative grammar.
extra: The linguist Leonard Bloomfield called it one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence.

q: Why were cane toads introduced to Australia in 1935?
opts: To control cane beetles in sugarcane crops
ans: To control cane beetles in sugarcane crops
why: They failed to control the beetles and instead spread widely and poisoned native predators.
extra: Toads at the invasion front have evolved longer legs.

q: Whose 1978 book Orientalism criticised Western representations of the East and helped found postcolonial studies?
why: Said argued that Western scholarship and literature constructed an exotic and inferior 'Orient' that served imperial power.
extra: He was a Palestinian-American professor at Columbia University.

q: What is the present temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation?
why: The radiation was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang and has been stretched by cosmic expansion to a cold 2.7 K.
extra: Penzias and Wilson detected it in 1965 and at first suspected the noise came from pigeon droppings in their antenna.

q: Which large spindle-shaped neurons, found in great apes, elephants and whales, are linked to social cognition?
why: These large bipolar cells occur in the anterior cingulate and fronto-insular cortex and may support rapid transmission of signals.
extra: They appear to have evolved independently in several large-brained lineages.

q: What produces the light in the lure of many deep-sea anglerfish?
why: The lure's bulb houses bacteria that glow, attracting prey in dark waters.
extra: In some species, tiny males fuse permanently to females.

q: Above roughly what mass can a white dwarf no longer be supported by electron degeneracy pressure, as calculated by Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar?
why: Beyond the Chandrasekhar limit, electron degeneracy pressure cannot resist gravity, so the star collapses or explodes. It becomes a neutron star or, in a binary, a Type Ia supernova.
extra: Chandrasekhar worked this out at about 19 years of age during his 1930 voyage from India to England, and won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

q: What is unusual about the Okavango Delta in Botswana?
opts: It is fed only by glacial meltwater
It is an inland delta that ends in the Kalahari rather than the sea
It flows uphill from the Indian Ocean
ans: It is an inland delta that ends in the Kalahari rather than the sea
why: The Okavango River spreads across Kalahari sands and its water is lost to evaporation and seepage instead of reaching an ocean. Its floods peak in the dry season because the rain falls months earlier in the Angolan highlands.
extra: The delta is one of the largest inland deltas in the world and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Common vampire bats regurgitate blood to feed roost-mates that failed to feed. This is mainly explained by what?
why: Bats are more likely to share with those who have shared with them, though relatives are also helped.
extra: Observations by Gerald Wilkinson in the 1980s showed it.

q: What did the 3.7-million-year-old Laetoli footprints in Tanzania show?
opts: Upright bipedal walking in early hominins
ans: Upright bipedal walking in early hominins
why: The footprints, preserved in volcanic ash and found by Mary Leakey's team, were made by a bipedal hominin, probably Australopithecus afarensis.
extra: They show that walking upright evolved long before brains became large.

q: Which compound, produced by soil bacteria such as Streptomyces, is largely responsible for the earthy smell after rain?
why: Raindrops hitting dry soil release tiny aerosols carrying geosmin and plant oils. Humans can detect geosmin at extraordinarily low concentrations.
extra: The word petrichor was coined in 1964 by Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas, and India's mitti attar from Kannauj captures this scent.

q: Which Western European language is a language isolate, unrelated to any other known language family?
why: Basque is spoken in the Pyrenees region and has no demonstrated relatives. It predates the arrival of Indo-European languages in Iberia.
extra: Proposed links to Caucasian or Iberian languages have not been accepted.

q: A person who consistently perceives colours when seeing letters or numbers is most likely experiencing which condition?
why: In synaesthesia, stimulation of one sensory or cognitive pathway automatically triggers an experience in another.
extra: Estimates suggest around 4% of people have some form of it.

q: According to the leading giant-impact hypothesis, how did the Moon form?
opts: By being captured from a passing planet
By fission of a rapidly rotating Earth
By accreting alongside Earth from the same disk
From debris after a Mars-sized body, Theia, struck the early Earth
ans: From debris after a Mars-sized body, Theia, struck the early Earth
why: A collision about 4.5 billion years ago would have thrown debris into orbit that coalesced into the Moon. Models explain its small iron core and the Earth-Moon angular momentum.
extra: Moon rocks are isotopically very similar to Earth's, which remains a puzzle for the hypothesis.

q: How many Earth-sized planets orbit the red dwarf TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away?
why: The TRAPPIST-1 system has seven rocky planets, several within or near the habitable zone. Its closely packed orbits are in resonance.
extra: JWST has been used to probe whether the inner planets have atmospheres.

q: Which spacecraft became the first to fly through the Sun's corona, in 2021?
why: Parker crossed the Alfven surface, the point where the solar wind decouples from the Sun, and sampled the corona directly.
extra: In December 2024 it passed within about 6.1 million km of the solar surface at roughly 690,000 km/h.

q: According to Stephen Hawking's 1974 result, what happens to an isolated black hole because of quantum effects near its horizon?
opts: It turns into a white hole
It slowly emits radiation and loses mass
ans: It slowly emits radiation and loses mass
why: Pairs of virtual particles near the horizon can lead to a net flow of radiation away from the hole. The hole's temperature is inversely proportional to its mass.
extra: Black holes of stellar mass are colder than the cosmic microwave background, so they currently gain more than they lose.

q: Which type of neutron star has the strongest known magnetic fields, up to around a thousand trillion gauss?
