why: Magnetars have fields about 1,000 times stronger than ordinary pulsars. Their decay powers bursts of X-rays and gamma-rays.
extra: The Milky Way magnetar SGR 1935+2154 produced a fast radio burst in 2020.

q: How many neurons does the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans have in its nervous system?
why: The hermaphrodite worm has exactly 302 neurons, and its complete wiring diagram was mapped in 1986.
extra: It was the first animal to have its whole connectome mapped.

q: The greater honeyguide is known for cooperating with humans in what way?
opts: Leading them to wild bees' nests, then feeding on the leftover wax and grubs
ans: Leading them to wild bees' nests, then feeding on the leftover wax and grubs
why: Honey-hunters use special calls and the birds respond by guiding them to nests.
extra: Studies in Mozambique show that calls used by Yao honey-hunters increase guiding.

q: A commonly cited estimate says that, on average, a language falls silent roughly how often?
why: Of the world's roughly 7,000 languages, about 40% are endangered. Language loss often follows shifts to dominant languages.
extra: Estimates vary, but the overall trend of rapid loss is well documented.

q: Which anthropologist popularised 'thick description' through his analysis of the Balinese cockfight?
why: Geertz argued that anthropologists should interpret the layered meanings of social actions, not just record behaviour. He borrowed the term from the philosopher Gilbert Ryle.
extra: His essay 'Deep Play' on the cockfight is one of the most cited in anthropology.

q: In 2022 India began reintroducing cheetahs from Namibia at which national park?
why: Kuno, in Madhya Pradesh, was chosen because of its habitat. The Asiatic cheetah had been declared extinct in India in 1952.
extra: Cubs were born in India in 2023.

q: Which critically endangered, ground-dwelling bird of the Thar was once proposed by Salim Ali as India's national bird?
why: The Great Indian Bustard survives mainly in Rajasthan and Gujarat, with only a small population left.
extra: Collisions with power lines are a major cause of death.

q: According to the standard Lambda-CDM model fitted to Planck satellite data, roughly what fraction of the Universe's energy content is dark energy?
why: Ordinary matter makes up about 5% and dark matter about 27%, leaving about 68% as dark energy. Its nature is unknown.
extra: The simplest explanation is a cosmological constant, a constant energy density of empty space.

q: Grid cells, which fire in a hexagonal pattern as an animal moves through space, were discovered in which brain region?
why: The Mosers found grid cells in the entorhinal cortex, providing a spatial coordinate system alongside the hippocampal place cells found by John O'Keefe.
extra: The three shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

q: What name is given to the brain's waste-clearance system, which is especially active during sleep?
why: Cerebrospinal fluid flows along channels around blood vessels and flushes out metabolites such as beta-amyloid.
extra: The glymphatic system was described by Maiken Nedergaard's group in 2012.

q: How deep did the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia reach, making it the deepest artificial point on Earth?
why: Drilling in the Kola Peninsula began in 1970 and reached about 12,262 m in 1989. It stopped because temperatures of around 180 degrees Celsius made the rock behave plastically and the drill bits failed.
extra: Scientists were surprised to find hot, mineral-rich water and microscopic plankton fossils deep in the hole.

q: Which sea has no coastline at all?
why: The Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic is bounded by ocean currents of the North Atlantic Gyre rather than by land. It is named after the floating Sargassum seaweed that gathers there.
extra: European and American eels both travel to the Sargasso Sea to spawn.

q: Roughly how far below sea level does the shore of the Dead Sea lie?
why: The Dead Sea shore, around 430 m below sea level, is the lowest exposed land elevation on Earth. The basin sits in the Jordan Rift Valley, a transform boundary between the Arabian and African plates.
extra: Its level is falling by more than a metre a year as Jordan River inflow is diverted.

q: If the Greenland ice sheet melted completely, global sea level would rise by about how much?
why: The Greenland ice sheet stores about 2.9 million cubic kilometres of ice, equivalent to roughly 7 m of sea level rise. This would take centuries to millennia.
extra: Antarctica's ice holds an equivalent of about 58 m of sea level.

q: Symmetrical magnetic stripes on either side of mid-ocean ridges provided evidence for what?
opts: Seafloor spreading and periodic reversals of Earth's magnetic field
ans: Seafloor spreading and periodic reversals of Earth's magnetic field
why: As new basalt forms at a ridge it records the magnetic field direction at the time, and the field has repeatedly reversed. The symmetric pattern confirmed that the seafloor grows outward from ridges.
extra: The idea was developed by Vine, Matthews and Morley in 1963.

q: What was the Inca khipu?
opts: A ritual trumpet made from a conch shell
A device of knotted cords used to record information
ans: A device of knotted cords used to record information
why: Khipus used knots and cord colours to encode numerical data in a decimal system, and some may have recorded other information. Specialists called khipukamayuq made and read them.
extra: The Incas had no conventional writing, so khipus were central to administration.

q: What is a 'whale fall'?
opts: A stranding event on a beach
A whale carcass on the seabed that supports a distinct deep-sea community for decades
ans: A whale carcass on the seabed that supports a distinct deep-sea community for decades
why: A carcass supports scavengers, then organisms that feed on enriched sediments, then bacteria that exploit sulfide from decomposing bone.
extra: Bone-eating worms of the genus Osedax feed on the bones.

q: Which Jorge Luis Borges story imagines a universe as an enormous library of hexagonal rooms holding every possible book?
why: Borges explored infinity and the limits of knowledge in this 1941 story, where books contain all possible combinations of characters.
extra: The library's books are each 410 pages long.

q: Which author instructed his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts, which Brod refused to do?
why: Brod published The Trial, The Castle and Amerika after Kafka's death in 1924.
extra: Kafka published very little during his life.

q: About how many neurons does the human brain contain?
why: Suzana Herculano-Houzel's isotropic fractionator method gave about 86 billion neurons, replacing the older estimate of 100 billion.
extra: About 16 billion of them are in the cerebral cortex.

q: Which hypothetical region is thought to be the source of long-period comets?
why: The Oort cloud is a vast spherical shell of icy bodies extending perhaps to 100,000 AU. Passing stars can nudge them inward as comets with periods of thousands of years.
extra: Short-period comets, like Halley's, mostly come from the Kuiper belt.

q: Which hypothesis proposes that the structure of a language influences the thought of its speakers?
why: The strong version, linguistic determinism, is largely rejected, but weaker influences on perception and memory have been supported.
extra: Examples include colour-discrimination studies and spatial language differences.

q: Cosmic inflation was proposed partly to explain which puzzle?
opts: Why the Hubble constant seems to vary
Why there is more matter than antimatter
Why distant regions of the Universe have almost the same temperature
ans: Why distant regions of the Universe have almost the same temperature
why: This is the horizon problem. A brief burst of exponential expansion would have brought regions into causal contact before stretching them apart.
extra: Alan Guth proposed inflation in 1981, which also addresses the flatness problem.

q: What mainly drives the deep sinking branch of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation?
opts: Cooling and sinking of dense, salty water in the North Atlantic
The pull of the Moon's tides
ans: Cooling and sinking of dense, salty water in the North Atlantic
why: Warm salty water flows north, cools, becomes dense and sinks near Greenland and the Nordic seas, then returns southward at depth. This transports heat and helps keep northwest Europe mild.
extra: Climate scientists monitor the circulation for signs of weakening as Greenland meltwater freshens the North Atlantic.

q: Which criterion did the IAU decide in 2006 that Pluto fails to meet as a planet?
opts: It is not massive enough to be round
It has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood
ans: It has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood
why: A planet must orbit the Sun, be nearly round and have cleared its orbit of other bodies. Pluto shares its region with many Kuiper belt objects.
extra: The discovery of Eris, slightly more massive than Pluto, helped prompt the decision.

q: In Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, what is the fictional town founded by the Buendia family?
why: Macondo is an isolated town that goes through boom, decline and apocalypse. The novel is a landmark of magical realism.
extra: Comala is from Rulfo's Pedro Paramo, Yoknapatawpha from Faulkner and Santa Maria from Onetti.

q: Which grammatical category marks how the speaker knows a piece of information, such as having seen it or heard it?
why: Languages such as Quechua and Turkish require speakers to mark the source of their information on verbs.
extra: In such languages, a statement lacking an evidential can sound incomplete.

q: Prosopagnosia, or face blindness, is most associated with dysfunction in which area?
why: Damage to the fusiform gyrus and connected areas impairs the ability to identify faces while leaving basic vision intact.
extra: Developmental prosopagnosia affects around 2% of people.

q: What did Vera Rubin's measurements of galaxy rotation curves reveal?
opts: Galaxies rotate backwards at their edges
Stars in outer regions orbit about as fast as inner ones, implying unseen mass
Galaxies have no central black holes
ans: Stars in outer regions orbit about as fast as inner ones, implying unseen mass
why: Visible matter alone predicts outer stars should orbit more slowly. The flat rotation curves implied extended halos of dark matter.
extra: Fritz Zwicky had hinted at missing mass in the Coma cluster in the 1930s.

q: Which light-sensitive protein in birds' retinas is a leading candidate for their magnetic compass sense?
why: The leading hypothesis proposes that light triggers radical-pair reactions in cryptochrome whose outcome depends on Earth's magnetic field direction.
extra: The mechanism is not yet established.

q: Who is considered the first named author in history, a priestess who wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna around 2300 BCE?
why: Enheduanna was a high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad.
extra: Her poems circulated for centuries after her death.

q: Which mountain range is the longest continental range on land?
why: The Andes run for about 7,000 km along the western edge of South America. They formed by subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate.
extra: The mid-ocean ridge system under the sea is far longer, at around 65,000 km.

q: Diamonds form deep in the mantle. Through eruptions of which rock type do they mainly reach the surface?
why: Kimberlite is a volatile-rich magma that rises from the mantle at great speed, carrying diamond-bearing fragments with it. The rapid ascent prevents the diamonds from turning to graphite.
extra: The name comes from Kimberley in South Africa, where the first major diamond mines were found.

q: Who discovered the first radio pulsar in 1967 as a Cambridge graduate student?
why: Bell noticed a regular series of pulses in chart-recorder data, at first nicknamed LGM-1 for little green men. They turned out to come from a rotating neutron star.
extra: The 1974 Nobel Prize went to Hewish and Ryle. In 2018 she donated her Breakthrough Prize money to support underrepresented physics students.

q: Which of these countries has an official Antarctic territorial claim?
why: Seven states claim Antarctic territory: the UK, Argentina, Chile, Norway, Australia, New Zealand and France. The US and Russia have reserved the right to claim but have not formally done so.
extra: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze these claims and banned military activity on the continent.

q: Whose black hole was the first to be imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019?
why: The image of M87's supermassive black hole, with a mass of about 6.5 billion Suns, showed a bright ring around a dark shadow. It lies roughly 55 million light-years away.
extra: The black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, Sagittarius A*, was imaged in 2022.

q: How does myelin speed up nerve conduction?
opts: It converts electrical signals into chemical ones
Impulses jump between the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction)
It pumps ions actively along the axon
ans: Impulses jump between the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction)
why: Myelin insulates the axon, so action potentials are regenerated only at gaps called nodes of Ranvier, allowing fast conduction.
extra: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that damages myelin in the central nervous system.

q: The default mode network is most active when a person is doing what?
opts: Resting or mind-wandering, not focused on an external task
Responding to a sudden loud noise
ans: Resting or mind-wandering, not focused on an external task
why: It includes midline and medial regions that are active during self-referential thought, remembering and imagining.
extra: Its activity patterns are altered in conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.

q: Why is the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region often called the Third Pole?
opts: It is the third-coldest place after Antarctica and Greenland
It holds the largest store of ice outside the polar regions
It has the third-strongest magnetic field
Earth's third rotation axis passes through it
ans: It holds the largest store of ice outside the polar regions
why: The region's glaciers and snowfields contain more ice than anywhere else outside the Arctic and Antarctic. Meltwater from them feeds rivers such as the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and Yangtze.
extra: The rivers fed by this ice support well over a billion people downstream.

q: What is the Capgras delusion?
opts: A belief that one is dead
A belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor
ans: A belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an impostor
why: People recognise the face but feel no emotional familiarity, and conclude the person must be a double.
extra: It has been linked to disconnection between face recognition and emotional processing.

q: ISRO's solar observatory Aditya-L1 was placed near which Sun-Earth Lagrange point?
why: L1 lies about 1.5 million km from Earth towards the Sun, giving an uninterrupted view of the Sun. The spacecraft reached its halo orbit around L1 in January 2024.
extra: The James Webb Space Telescope is at L2, on the opposite side.

q: How do dolphins sleep without drowning?
opts: One brain hemisphere sleeps at a time
They do not sleep at all
They sleep only on the sea floor
ans: One brain hemisphere sleeps at a time
why: This unihemispheric slow-wave sleep keeps one hemisphere awake so the animal can surface to breathe and watch for threats.
extra: The same is seen in some seals and birds.

q: Which novel won the Booker Prize in 1981, the 'Booker of Bookers' in 1993 and the 'Best of the Booker' in 2008?
why: Salman Rushdie's novel follows Saleem Sinai, born at the midnight of Indian independence, whose life mirrors the nation's.
extra: Rushdie's novel is a leading example of magical realism in Indian English.

q: Which of these English words comes from Hindi?
why: Shampoo comes from Hindi champo, meaning to press or knead. Safari is from Arabic via Swahili, tsunami from Japanese and kayak from Inuit.
extra: Loot, jungle and pyjamas are also from Indian languages.

q: The 1947 Radcliffe Line partitioned which two provinces of British India?
why: Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India before, drew the boundaries within about five weeks, dividing Punjab and Bengal along religious majorities. The award was made public on 17 August 1947, two days after independence.
extra: The line became the India-Pakistan and India-Bangladesh border in those regions.

q: Which language was revived from mainly religious use to become an everyday spoken language in the 19th and 20th centuries?
why: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others promoted Hebrew in Palestine, coining new words and making it a mother tongue for new generations.
extra: Very few languages have been revived as native community languages on this scale.

q: According to Bowen's reaction series, which common mineral crystallises first from cooling mafic magma at high temperature?
why: Olivine forms at the highest temperatures and is followed by pyroxene, amphibole and biotite as the melt cools. Quartz and muscovite crystallise at the end.
extra: This is why olivine is common in basalt and in the upper mantle, but rare in granite.

q: In Kalidasa's Meghaduta, to whom does an exiled yaksha entrust his message for his beloved?
why: The yaksha asks a monsoon cloud to carry his message across India and describes the route in lyrical detail.
extra: It started a genre of Sanskrit 'messenger poems' (sandesha kavya).

q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
why: Largely because of its vast Arctic archipelago, Canada's coastline exceeds 200,000 km, more than any other country's. Norway's fjords and islands also make its coast far longer than its straight-line extent suggests.
extra: Coastlines illustrate the coastline paradox: measured length grows as the measuring scale gets finer.

q: How did Nicaraguan Sign Language arise?
opts: Deaf children brought together in schools in the 1970s and 80s spontaneously developed it
Missionaries imported it from American Sign Language
ans: Deaf children brought together in schools in the 1970s and 80s spontaneously developed it
why: Children who had no shared language developed a gesture system and later younger cohorts turned it into a fully grammatical language.
extra: It provides evidence that children create linguistic structure.

q: What was notable about India's Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), launched in 2013?
opts: It found fossil life on Mars
It made the first landing on Mars by an Asian country
India became the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt
ans: India became the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt
why: The orbiter entered Mars orbit in September 2014 on its first try, at a cost of well under 100 million US dollars.
extra: It operated far longer than its planned six months.

q: Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram, in August 2023, made India the first country to achieve what?
opts: A sample return from the Moon's far side
A soft landing near the Moon's south polar region
ans: A soft landing near the Moon's south polar region
why: The lander touched down on 23 August 2023 at about 69 degrees south, farther south than any earlier soft landing. Its rover Pragyan measured the lunar surface composition.
extra: India became the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China.

q: Which poet's real name was Mirza Asadullah Baig Khan?
why: Ghalib wrote in Urdu and Persian in Delhi in the 19th century and served at the Mughal court of Bahadur Shah Zafar.
extra: He is celebrated for his ghazals.

q: Which fungus manipulates the behaviour of carpenter ants, making them climb and clamp onto vegetation before they die?
why: The fungus grows through the ant's body and causes it to bite plant veins in a spot favourable for spore dispersal.
extra: Different Ophiocordyceps species target different ant species.

q: Within the first few minutes after the Big Bang, which elements were mainly produced?
why: Big Bang nucleosynthesis ended when the Universe cooled too much for fusion. Heavier elements formed later in stars and stellar explosions.
extra: The predicted helium fraction of about 25% by mass matches observations.

q: Which of these is the oldest known surviving epic poem?
why: Parts of Gilgamesh were written in Sumerian around 2100 BCE and the standard Akkadian version later.
extra: Tablet XI contains a flood narrative with parallels to the biblical story.

q: Which jellyfish can revert from adult medusa to polyp stage, potentially cycling indefinitely?
why: The process, transdifferentiation, lets cells change their identity, effectively resetting development.
extra: In the wild, it can still die by predation and disease.

q: In the deep ocean, a tsunami travels at roughly what speed?
why: A tsunami's speed is set by water depth, approximately the square root of gravity times depth. In a 4,000 m deep ocean that works out to the speed of a jet airliner.
extra: In deep water the wave is typically under a metre high, but it slows and grows as it reaches shallow coasts.

q: True or false: a day on Venus (one rotation) is longer than its year.
why: Venus rotates once every about 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in about 225 days. Its rotation is also retrograde, opposite to most planets.
extra: Because of the retrograde spin, the Sun rises in the west and the solar day lasts about 117 Earth days.

q: Which writer, born Dhanpat Rai, wrote the Hindi novel Godaan (1936)?
why: Premchand began writing in Urdu as Nawab Rai and turned to Hindi later. Godaan portrays a poor peasant, Hori, and rural exploitation.
extra: He is regarded as a pioneer of social realism in Hindi and Urdu fiction.

q: The Siddi communities of Gujarat and Karnataka are largely descended from people brought from where?
why: Siddis descend mainly from Bantu-speaking Africans brought to India as soldiers, sailors and enslaved people by Arab, Portuguese and other traders. They now speak languages such as Gujarati, Konkani and Kannada.
extra: Malik Ambar, born in Ethiopia, rose to become a powerful military leader in the Ahmednagar Sultanate.

q: What are fast radio bursts?
opts: Millisecond-long radio flashes, mostly from distant galaxies
ans: Millisecond-long radio flashes, mostly from distant galaxies
why: FRBs release in milliseconds as much energy as the Sun emits in days. Some repeat, and their origins are still being studied.
extra: The 2020 burst from a Galactic magnetar supports a magnetar origin for at least some of them.

q: Robert Paine's experiments removing which predator from Pacific tide pools led to the 'keystone species' concept?
why: Removing the sea star let mussels dominate and crowd out other species, and diversity collapsed.
extra: Paine coined the term 'keystone species' in 1969.

q: Studies of London taxi drivers by Eleanor Maguire found enlargement of which brain region with navigational experience?
why: Taxi drivers who had memorised the city's streets had larger posterior hippocampi, and the size correlated with years on the job.
extra: It suggests the adult human brain retains structural plasticity.

q: The sharing of features such as retroflex consonants and subject-object-verb word order across unrelated South Asian language families is an example of what?
why: Murray Emeneau described South Asia as a linguistic area in 1956. Contact over millennia led Indo-Aryan, Dravidian and others to converge.
extra: Retroflex consonants may have spread to Indo-Aryan from Dravidian.

q: Which Spanish work, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, is often called the first modern European novel?
why: Cervantes parodied chivalric romances. In Part Two, the characters know that Part One has been published.
extra: He claims the story comes from a fictional Arab historian, Cide Hamete Benengeli.

q: A creole language arises when what happens?
opts: A pidgin becomes the native language of a community's children
A language is simplified by a government
ans: A pidgin becomes the native language of a community's children
why: Pidgins are simplified contact languages. When children acquire them as first languages, they expand into full languages with complex grammar.
extra: Tok Pisin and Haitian Creole are examples.

q: In which year did Voyager 1 cross the heliopause into interstellar space?
why: Voyager 1 detected a jump in plasma density in August 2012 showing that it had left the Sun's heliosphere. Its twin Voyager 2 did so in 2018.
extra: Voyager 1 is now more than 160 times as far from the Sun as Earth.

q: Dmanisi, which has yielded 1.8-million-year-old Homo erectus fossils, is located in which country?
why: The Dmanisi hominins, found in the Caucasus, are among the earliest known human relatives outside Africa. Some show small brains and primitive features.
extra: The skulls show wide variation, leading some researchers to argue that early Homo may have fewer species than once thought.

q: True or false: Russia's Big Diomede Island and the United States' Little Diomede Island are less than 5 km apart.
why: The two islands in the Bering Strait are about 3.8 km apart, and both the international boundary and the International Date Line run between them.
extra: Because of the Date Line, Big Diomede is roughly a day ahead of Little Diomede, which gave rise to the nicknames Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Island.

q: In Hindi, the consonant ट differs from त mainly in which respect?
opts: ट is retroflex, while त is dental
ट is palatal and त is uvular
ट is a nasal and त is a stop
ट is voiced and त is voiceless
ans: ट is retroflex, while त is dental
why: In retroflex sounds, the tongue tip is curled back towards the palate, while in dental sounds the tongue touches the teeth.
extra: English speakers typically map both onto an alveolar t.

q: What is unusual about the migration of the North American monarch butterfly?
opts: The round trip takes several generations
ans: The round trip takes several generations
why: The overwintering generation lives for months, while generations that breed on the way north live only a few weeks.
extra: The butterflies navigate using a time-compensated sun compass.

q: A 'supereruption' is classed as which value on the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
why: VEI 8 eruptions eject more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material. They are far rarer than VEI 7 events such as Tambora in 1815.
extra: The Toba eruption in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago was a VEI 8 event.

q: Which empirical law states that a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its frequency rank?
why: The most frequent word occurs about twice as often as the second, three times as often as the third, and so on.
extra: In English, 'the' is usually the most frequent word.

q: Which small reef fish has passed a version of the mirror self-recognition test?
why: Some cleaner wrasse examined and tried to remove a mark on their throats that was visible only in a mirror.
extra: The meaning of this result for self-awareness is debated.

q: Which glial cells act as the brain's resident immune cells and prune synapses during development?
why: Microglia clear debris and eliminate weak synapses, shaping neural circuits.
extra: They are also implicated in neurodegenerative diseases.

q: Which sound law explains why Latin 'pater' corresponds to English 'father', with p becoming f?
why: Grimm's law describes regular consonant shifts in Germanic, including p to f, t to th and k to h.
extra: Jacob Grimm, who formulated it, also collected fairy tales with his brother Wilhelm.

q: Which two countries each share land borders with 14 other countries, more than any others?
why: China and Russia are tied for the most land neighbours. Brazil has 10 and Germany has 9, so they trail.
extra: Many of China's and Russia's borders run through Central and East Asia, where the frontiers are long and varied.

q: Whose giant axon allowed Hodgkin and Huxley to work out the ionic basis of the action potential in 1952?
why: The squid giant axon is about a millimetre wide, large enough for electrodes. They explained the action potential through sodium and potassium currents.
extra: They shared the 1963 Nobel Prize with John Eccles.

q: Which Indian island holds the only confirmed active volcano in the country?
why: Barren Island, in the Andaman Sea, is part of the volcanic arc formed by subduction of the Indian plate beneath the Burma microplate. It has erupted repeatedly since 1991.
extra: Narcondam, nearby, is classed as dormant.

q: What forms the base of the food web at deep-sea hydrothermal vents?
opts: Chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidise hydrogen sulfide
ans: Chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidise hydrogen sulfide
why: Bacteria use chemical energy from vent fluids to fix carbon and often live symbiotically in tube worms and clams.
extra: Vent communities were discovered near the Galapagos in 1977.

q: Which 1798 collection by Wordsworth and Coleridge is often seen as launching English Romanticism?
why: The book aimed to use ordinary language and rustic subjects, as explained in Wordsworth's later preface.
extra: It included Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner.

q: Whose discovery of the period-luminosity relation of Cepheid variables allowed astronomers to measure distances to other galaxies?
why: Leavitt noticed in 1912, studying variable stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, that brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly. This provided a yardstick for cosmic distances.
extra: Hubble used Cepheids in Andromeda to show it lies outside the Milky Way.

q: What was atmospherically unusual about the January 2022 eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai?
opts: It injected a record amount of water vapour into the stratosphere
It produced the largest lava flow in recorded history
It released more sulfur dioxide than any eruption on record
It destroyed the ozone layer over the entire Pacific
ans: It injected a record amount of water vapour into the stratosphere
why: The undersea eruption blasted seawater high into the stratosphere, adding on the order of ten percent to the stratosphere's water vapour. That is an unprecedented perturbation for an eruption.
extra: Its atmospheric shockwave travelled around the globe several times and was recorded by barometers worldwide.

q: In the McGurk effect, what happens when a person sees a mouth saying one syllable while hearing another?
opts: They hear both syllables in sequence
They perceive a third, blended syllable
They hear only the visual syllable
ans: They perceive a third, blended syllable
why: Vision and audition are combined automatically in speech perception, so a mismatch yields a fused percept.
extra: The effect shows that speech perception is multisensory.

q: The Mohorovicic discontinuity marks the boundary between which two layers?
why: The Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic identified in 1909 a sudden jump in seismic wave speed at the base of the crust. That jump marks the transition from crust to mantle.
extra: Oceanic crust is only about 7 km thick, while continental crust is typically 30 to 50 km thick.

q: Which poet completed the Shahnameh, about 50,000 couplets, around 1010 CE?
why: The Shahnameh preserves Persian legends and history from the mythical past to the Arab conquest.
extra: It is widely credited with helping to sustain the Persian language.

q: Berlin and Kay's 1969 study of colour terms proposed that languages acquire basic colour words in what pattern?
opts: In random order depending on climate
In a roughly universal order, beginning with dark and light, then red
ans: In a roughly universal order, beginning with dark and light, then red
why: They argued that languages with few colour terms distinguish dark and light, and add terms in a fairly constrained sequence, for instance red before green or blue.
extra: Later critics questioned the universality of the sequence.

q: Which scientist argued, using Golgi's stain, that the nervous system consists of discrete cells?
why: Cajal's neuron doctrine held that neurons are separate cells, while Golgi favoured a continuous reticular network.
extra: They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize despite disagreeing.

q: About how many neurons were mapped in the complete adult fruit fly brain connectome published in 2024?
why: The FlyWire project mapped roughly 140,000 neurons and around 50 million synapses.
extra: It is the largest complete adult-brain connectome so far.

q: In 2022 JWST made the first clear detection of which molecule in an exoplanet atmosphere, that of WASP-39 b?
why: WASP-39 b is a hot gas giant about 700 light-years away. JWST's transmission spectrum showed a distinct carbon dioxide feature.
extra: The same observations found evidence of sulfur dioxide made by photochemistry, another first.

q: Wolfram Schultz's recordings showed that midbrain dopamine neurons encode what?
opts: The absolute size of a reward
why: The neurons fire for unexpected rewards and fall silent when an expected reward is omitted, signalling the difference between expected and received outcomes.
extra: This matches temporal-difference learning algorithms used in reinforcement learning.

q: In which language did Tulsidas compose the Ramcharitmanas in the 16th century?
why: It is a retelling of the Ramayana in the vernacular, which made the story accessible to ordinary people.
extra: It underlies many Ramlila performances across North India.

q: Which mountain's summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's centre?
why: Earth bulges at the equator because of its rotation, so Ecuador's equatorial Chimborazo is farther from the centre than Everest, even though Everest is far higher above sea level.
extra: Chimborazo's summit is roughly 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's.

q: Which bird is famous for flying over the Himalaya during migration, at altitudes of up to around 7,000 m?
why: The bar-headed goose has haemoglobin with high oxygen affinity and efficient lungs for flying in thin air.
extra: It winters in India and breeds in Central Asia.

q: Fossils of which Permian seed fern, found in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, supported Wegener's continental drift hypothesis?
why: Glossopteris had heavy seeds that could not have crossed wide oceans, so its distribution suggests those lands were once joined as Gondwana.
extra: The freshwater reptile Mesosaurus, found only in South America and Africa, is a classic companion line of evidence.

q: Roughly how much would a teaspoonful of neutron star material weigh?
why: A neutron star packs more than a solar mass into a sphere about 20 km across, with a density of hundreds of trillions of grams per cubic centimetre.
extra: This is comparable to the density of an atomic nucleus.

q: Who showed in 1936 that Earth has a solid inner core inside the liquid outer core?
why: Lehmann, a Danish seismologist, noticed faint P-waves arriving where the liquid-core model predicted none, and explained them as reflections from a solid inner core.
extra: Her inference was confirmed in the 1970s using more sensitive seismographs.

q: The 2017 detection of the neutron star merger GW170817 showed that such mergers can forge which heavy elements?
why: The afterglow, called a kilonova, had spectra indicating rapid neutron-capture products. Such mergers are thus a major source of the heaviest elements.
extra: It was the first event observed in both gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation.

q: The reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone in 1995 is the classic example of what ecological process?
why: Wolves reduced elk numbers and changed their behaviour, which allowed streamside vegetation to recover.
extra: The magnitude of the effects on rivers and other aspects is debated.

q: Biomagnification of DDT in the 20th century caused thinning of eggshells in which birds?
opts: Top predators such as peregrine falcons and bald eagles
ans: Top predators such as peregrine falcons and bald eagles
why: DDT accumulates up food chains, and the metabolite DDE interferes with eggshell calcium deposition in birds of prey.
extra: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) drew attention to this problem.

q: According to tradition, why was the Panchatantra composed?
opts: To entertain a king's guests at feasts
To teach princes statecraft through fables
ans: To teach princes statecraft through fables
why: Vishnu Sharma is said to have used animal tales to educate three unruly princes in politics and conduct.
extra: It was translated into Pahlavi around the 6th century and later spread to Europe as Kalila wa Dimna.

q: Silbo Gomero is a whistled form of which language, used on La Gomera in the Canary Islands?
why: Whistlers replace the spoken sounds of Spanish with whistled pitches and rhythms that carry across deep ravines.
extra: UNESCO recognised it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

q: On which date, commemorated as Bloomsday, is the action of James Joyce's Ulysses set?
why: Joyce chose the date of his first outing with Nora Barnacle. The novel follows Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin.
extra: The novel was published in 1922 and parallels Homer's Odyssey.

q: What is the 'Hubble tension'?
opts: Strain between galaxy clusters due to gravity
A mismatch between local measurements of the expansion rate and predictions from the early Universe

q: When did Earth's magnetic field last undergo a full polarity reversal?
why: The Brunhes-Matuyama reversal, about 780,000 years ago, is the most recent full flip of the geomagnetic field. Reversals occur at irregular intervals, averaging several per million years.
extra: The Laschamps excursion about 41,000 years ago was a brief, incomplete weakening and shift of the field.

q: Roughly how many times longer than the Iliad and the Odyssey combined is the Mahabharata?
why: The Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to Vyasa, has about 100,000 verses and well over a million words, making it among the longest epics ever composed.
extra: The Bhagavad Gita is a short section within its Bhishma Parva.

q: Damage to Wernicke's area typically produces which kind of speech problem?
opts: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension
ans: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension
why: People with Wernicke's aphasia speak smoothly, but their words often make no sense and they struggle to understand language.
extra: Broca's area damage causes the opposite pattern, with effortful, non-fluent speech.

q: What typically happens in the equatorial Pacific during an El Nino event?
opts: Sea level rises in the western Pacific
Trade winds strengthen and cold water upwells more strongly
Trade winds weaken and warm water shifts eastward
The thermocline deepens in the west
ans: Trade winds weaken and warm water shifts eastward
why: Weaker trade winds allow the western Pacific warm pool to spread east, suppressing upwelling off South America. This shifts rainfall patterns across the globe.
extra: El Nino is often associated with weaker Indian summer monsoon rainfall, although the link is not consistent every year.
